description: Comprehensive Biology question bank derived from the provided Biology.pdf study material, formatted for KEA examination preparation. Questions cover all sections: Introduction to Biology, Cell Biology, Human Anatomy and Physiology, Nutrition and Human Health, Diseases and Public Health, Genetics and Evolution, Plant Biology, Microbiology, and Animal Biology and Zoology.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is biology?

options.A: The study of matter and energy
options.B: The scientific study of life and living organisms
options.C: The study of rocks and minerals

questions.explanation: Biology is the scientific study of life and living organisms, including their structure, functions, growth, origin, evolution, distribution and interactions.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which branch of biology is concerned with plants?

options.A: Zoology
options.B: Microbiology

questions.explanation: Botany is the branch of biology concerned with plants, including their structure, physiology, classification, reproduction and ecology.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which branch of biology deals with animals?

options.A: Botany
options.B: Zoology

questions.explanation: Zoology is the branch of biology concerned with animals, including their structure, physiology, behaviour, classification and evolution.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is microbiology?

options.A: The study of large animals
options.B: The study of microorganisms such as bacteria, fungi, protozoa and viruses

questions.explanation: Microbiology is the study of microorganisms such as bacteria, many fungi, protozoa, microscopic algae and viruses.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is biotechnology?

options.A: The study of fossils
options.B: The application of organisms, cells or biological molecules to develop products and processes

questions.explanation: Biotechnology is the application of organisms, cells or biological molecules to develop products and processes, such as vaccines, fermented foods, enzymes and improved crops.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is genetics?

options.A: The study of heredity and variation
options.B: The study of ecosystems

questions.explanation: Genetics is the study of heredity and variation, including genes, DNA, chromosomes and inheritance.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is ecology?

options.A: The study of cells
options.B: The study of interactions among organisms and between organisms and their physical environment

questions.explanation: Ecology is the study of interactions among organisms and between organisms and their physical environment.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is anatomy?

options.A: The study of how organs function
options.B: The study of the internal and external structure of organisms

questions.explanation: Anatomy is the study of the internal and external structure of organisms and their body parts.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is physiology?

options.A: The study of body structure
options.B: The study of how living organisms and their organs, tissues and cells function

questions.explanation: Physiology is the study of how living organisms and their organs, tissues and cells function.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is taxonomy?

options.A: The science of identifying, naming and classifying organisms
options.B: The study of cells

questions.explanation: Taxonomy is the science of identifying, naming and classifying organisms.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are the main taxonomic ranks in biological classification from broadest to most specific?

options.A: Kingdom, Domain, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species
options.B: Domain, Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species
options.C: Phylum, Kingdom, Domain, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species
options.D: Domain, Phylum, Kingdom, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species

questions.explanation: The main taxonomic ranks are Domain, Kingdom, Phylum (division in plants), Class, Order, Family, Genus and Species.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Who proposed the five-kingdom classification?

options.A: Carl Linnaeus
options.B: R. H. Whittaker

questions.explanation: R. H. Whittaker proposed the five-kingdom classification in 1969.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which kingdoms are included in Whittaker's five-kingdom classification?

options.A: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia
options.B: Bacteria, Archaea, Eukarya, Plantae, Animalia

questions.explanation: Whittaker's five-kingdom system divides organisms into Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What organisms are placed in Kingdom Monera?

options.A: Eukaryotic organisms with cell walls
options.B: Prokaryotic organisms, including bacteria and cyanobacteria

questions.explanation: Kingdom Monera includes prokaryotic organisms, including bacteria and cyanobacteria; archaea were historically grouped here but are now recognised as a distinct domain.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What organisms are placed in Kingdom Protista?

options.A: Prokaryotic organisms only
options.B: Mostly unicellular eukaryotes such as Amoeba and Paramecium

questions.explanation: Kingdom Protista includes mostly unicellular eukaryotes, such as Amoeba, Paramecium and many unicellular algae.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are the main characteristics of Kingdom Fungi?

options.A: Prokaryotic, photosynthetic organisms
options.B: Eukaryotic organisms that absorb nutrients, usually have chitin-containing cell walls and reproduce by spores
options.D: Unicellular organisms with cellulose cell walls

questions.explanation: Kingdom Fungi includes eukaryotic organisms that absorb nutrients, usually have chitin-containing cell walls and commonly reproduce by spores.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are the main characteristics of Kingdom Plantae?

options.A: Prokaryotic organisms with peptidoglycan walls
options.B: Mostly multicellular eukaryotes with cellulose cell walls; many contain chlorophyll and carry out photosynthesis
options.C: Multicellular organisms that obtain nutrients by ingestion
options.D: Eukaryotic organisms that absorb nutrients and have chitin walls

questions.explanation: Kingdom Plantae includes mostly multicellular eukaryotes with cellulose cell walls; many contain chlorophyll and carry out photosynthesis.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are the main characteristics of Kingdom Animalia?

options.A: Multicellular eukaryotes without cell walls that obtain nutrients by ingestion
options.B: Multicellular eukaryotes with cellulose cell walls

questions.explanation: Kingdom Animalia includes multicellular eukaryotes without cell walls that obtain nutrients by ingestion; most show movement at some life stage.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is binomial nomenclature?

options.A: A two-part scientific naming system with genus and species names
options.B: A classification system with five kingdoms

questions.explanation: Binomial nomenclature is the two-part scientific naming system in which each species has a genus name followed by a specific epithet; names are Latin or latinised and conventionally italicised.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Who popularised binomial nomenclature?

options.A: Charles Darwin
options.B: Carl Linnaeus

questions.explanation: Carl Linnaeus, the Swedish naturalist, systematised and popularised the modern binomial naming system.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the scientific name of human beings?

options.A: Homo sapiens
options.B: Canis lupus familiaris

questions.explanation: The scientific name of human beings is Homo sapiens.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the scientific name of the mango?

options.A: Oryza sativa
options.B: Triticum aestivum

questions.explanation: The scientific name of the mango is Mangifera indica.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the scientific name of rice?

options.A: Triticum aestivum
options.B: Oryza sativa

questions.explanation: The scientific name of rice is Oryza sativa.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the scientific name of the neem tree?

options.A: Mangifera indica
options.B: Oryza sativa

questions.explanation: The scientific name of the neem tree is Azadirachta indica.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the scientific name of the housefly?

options.A: Drosophila melanogaster
options.B: Musca domestica

questions.explanation: The scientific name of the housefly is Musca domestica.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the scientific name of the fruit fly commonly used in genetics?

options.A: Musca domestica
options.B: Drosophila melanogaster

questions.explanation: The scientific name of the fruit fly commonly used in genetics is Drosophila melanogaster.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are the principal characteristics of living organisms?

options.A: Cellular organisation, metabolism, growth, reproduction, response to stimuli, homeostasis, adaptation and evolution
options.B: Only growth and reproduction
options.D: Only response to stimuli and adaptation

questions.explanation: The principal characteristics of living organisms include cellular organisation, metabolism, growth, reproduction, response to stimuli, homeostasis, adaptation and evolution; no single feature alone is sufficient to define all life in every case.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is metabolism?

options.A: The sum of all chemical reactions in an organism
options.B: The process of cell division
options.C: The maintenance of stable internal conditions

questions.explanation: Metabolism is the sum of all chemical reactions in an organism; anabolism builds complex molecules and catabolism breaks molecules down.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is homeostasis?

options.A: The process of reproduction
options.B: The maintenance of relatively stable internal conditions

questions.explanation: Homeostasis is the maintenance of relatively stable internal conditions, such as body temperature, blood glucose and water balance, despite external changes.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Are viruses considered living organisms?

options.A: Yes, because they can reproduce independently
options.B: No, because they are acellular and cannot reproduce independently; they replicate only inside host cells
options.C: Yes, because they have cellular organisation
options.D: No, because they lack genetic material

questions.explanation: Viruses are acellular and cannot reproduce independently; they replicate only inside host cells. Whether they are classified as living is debated, so many biology texts describe them as being at the boundary of living and non-living.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Who first observed cells?

options.A: Antoine van Leeuwenhoek
options.B: Robert Hooke

questions.explanation: Robert Hooke described tiny compartments in cork and coined the term 'cells' in 1665.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Who first observed living microorganisms?

options.A: Robert Hooke
options.B: Antoine van Leeuwenhoek

questions.explanation: Antoine van Leeuwenhoek, using microscopes in the 1670s, observed bacteria and other microscopic organisms.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What does the classical cell theory state?

options.A: All living organisms are made of one or more cells, the cell is the basic unit of structure and function, and cells arise from pre-existing cells
options.B: All cells contain a nucleus
options.D: Cells can arise spontaneously from non-living matter

questions.explanation: The classical cell theory states that all living organisms are made of one or more cells, the cell is the basic unit of structure and function, and cells arise from pre-existing cells.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Who formulated the original cell theory?

options.A: Robert Hooke and Antoine van Leeuwenhoek
options.B: Matthias Schleiden and Theodor Schwann

questions.explanation: Matthias Schleiden and Theodor Schwann formulated the original cell theory in 1838-1839; Rudolf Virchow later popularised the principle that cells arise from pre-existing cells.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a cell?

options.A: A group of tissues
options.B: The basic structural, functional and biological unit of life

questions.explanation: A cell is the basic structural, functional and biological unit of life.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the plasma membrane?

options.A: A rigid outer layer found in all cells
options.B: A selectively permeable phospholipid bilayer with proteins that surrounds the cell

questions.explanation: The plasma membrane is a selectively permeable phospholipid bilayer with proteins that surrounds the cell and regulates movement of substances into and out of it.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the composition of plant cell walls?

options.A: Chitin
options.B: Peptidoglycan

questions.explanation: Plant cell walls are mainly cellulose, together with hemicelluloses and pectins; secondary walls may also contain lignin.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the main composition of fungal cell walls?

options.A: Cellulose
options.B: Chitin

questions.explanation: Fungal cell walls contain chitin; bacterial walls usually contain peptidoglycan, and plant cell walls are mainly cellulose.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the main composition of bacterial cell walls?

options.A: Cellulose
options.B: Chitin

questions.explanation: Bacterial cell walls usually contain peptidoglycan.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is cytoplasm?

options.A: The region between the plasma membrane and nucleus in a typical eukaryotic cell, containing cytosol and organelles
options.B: The membrane-bound organelle containing DNA
options.C: The rigid outer layer of plant cells

questions.explanation: Cytoplasm is the region between the plasma membrane and nucleus in a typical eukaryotic cell, containing cytosol and organelles.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the nucleus?

options.A: The site of ATP production
options.B: A membrane-bound organelle in eukaryotic cells that contains most of the cell's DNA

questions.explanation: The nucleus is a membrane-bound organelle in eukaryotic cells that contains most of the cell's DNA and regulates gene expression and cellular activities.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the nucleolus?

options.A: A dense region inside the nucleus where ribosomal RNA is made and ribosomal subunits begin to assemble
options.B: The membrane surrounding the nucleus

questions.explanation: The nucleolus is a dense region inside the nucleus where ribosomal RNA is made and ribosomal subunits begin to assemble.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are chromosomes?

options.A: Structures of DNA associated with proteins that carry genes and transmit hereditary information
options.B: Membrane-bound organelles that produce ATP

questions.explanation: Chromosomes are structures of DNA associated with proteins that carry genes and transmit hereditary information.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Why are mitochondria called the powerhouse of the cell?

options.A: Because they synthesise proteins
options.B: Because they produce much of the ATP used to power cellular processes through aerobic respiration
options.D: Because they package proteins for secretion

questions.explanation: Mitochondria are called the powerhouse of the cell because they produce much of the ATP used to power cellular processes through aerobic respiration; the phrase is a useful simplification.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are ribosomes?

options.A: Double-membraned organelles that produce ATP
options.B: Small complexes of ribosomal RNA and proteins that translate messenger RNA to synthesise proteins
options.D: Organelles that modify and package proteins

questions.explanation: Ribosomes are small complexes of ribosomal RNA and proteins that translate messenger RNA to synthesise proteins; they occur in both prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the function of rough endoplasmic reticulum?

options.A: Lipid synthesis and detoxification
options.B: Synthesis and processing of proteins

questions.explanation: Rough ER has ribosomes and is involved in synthesis/processing of proteins; smooth ER is involved in lipid synthesis, detoxification and calcium storage.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the function of smooth endoplasmic reticulum?

options.A: Protein synthesis
options.B: Lipid synthesis, detoxification and calcium storage

questions.explanation: Smooth ER is involved in lipid synthesis, detoxification and calcium storage.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the function of the Golgi apparatus?

options.A: ATP production
options.B: Modifies, sorts and packages proteins and lipids into vesicles for transport or secretion

questions.explanation: The Golgi apparatus is an organelle that modifies, sorts and packages proteins and lipids into vesicles for transport or secretion.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are lysosomes?

options.A: Membrane-bound organelles containing digestive enzymes that break down cellular waste and macromolecules
options.B: Organelles that produce ATP
options.D: Organelles that modify and package proteins

questions.explanation: Lysosomes are membrane-bound organelles containing digestive enzymes that break down cellular waste, macromolecules and worn-out organelles; they are especially prominent in many animal cells.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the function of the large central vacuole in plant cells?

options.A: Protein synthesis
options.B: Storage and maintenance of turgor pressure

questions.explanation: Plant cells commonly have a large central vacuole that helps maintain turgor pressure and serves storage functions.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are plastids?

options.A: Double-membraned organelles in plants and algae, including chloroplasts, chromoplasts and leucoplasts
options.B: Membrane-bound organelles containing digestive enzymes
options.C: Sites of protein synthesis in bacteria
options.D: Organelles that modify and package proteins

questions.explanation: Plastids are double-membraned organelles in plants and algae, including chloroplasts, chromoplasts and leucoplasts.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Where does photosynthesis occur in plant cells?

options.A: Mitochondria
options.B: Chloroplasts

questions.explanation: Chloroplasts are plastids containing chlorophyll where photosynthesis occurs in plants and many algae; they have thylakoid membranes and a stroma.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the main difference between plant and animal cells?

options.A: Plant cells have a nucleus; animal cells do not
options.B: Typical plant cells have a cellulose cell wall, plastids and a large central vacuole; typical animal cells lack a cell wall and plastids
options.C: Animal cells have chloroplasts; plant cells do not
options.D: Plant cells lack mitochondria; animal cells have them

questions.explanation: Typical plant cells have a cellulose cell wall, plastids and a large central vacuole; typical animal cells lack a cell wall and plastids and often have prominent lysosomes and centrioles.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a prokaryotic cell?

options.A: A cell with a membrane-bound nucleus and membrane-bound organelles
options.B: A cell without a membrane-bound nucleus or membrane-bound organelles; its DNA is located in a nucleoid region

questions.explanation: A prokaryotic cell is a cell without a membrane-bound nucleus or membrane-bound organelles; its DNA is located in a nucleoid region. Bacteria and archaea are prokaryotes.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a eukaryotic cell?

options.A: A cell without a nucleus
options.B: A cell with a membrane-bound nucleus and membrane-bound organelles
options.D: A cell found only in bacteria

questions.explanation: A eukaryotic cell is a cell with a membrane-bound nucleus and membrane-bound organelles; plants, animals, fungi and protists are eukaryotes.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a unicellular organism?

options.A: An organism composed of many specialised cells
options.B: An organism consisting of a single cell that performs all essential life functions
options.D: An organism with a nucleus but no organelles

questions.explanation: A unicellular organism consists of a single cell that performs all essential life functions; examples include bacteria, Amoeba and many yeasts.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a multicellular organism?

options.A: An organism consisting of a single cell
options.B: An organism composed of many cells that may be specialised and organised into tissues, organs and organ systems
options.D: An organism that lacks cell walls

questions.explanation: A multicellular organism is composed of many cells that may be specialised and organised into tissues, organs and organ systems.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is cell division?

options.A: The process by which a parent cell divides to form daughter cells
options.B: The process of cell death

questions.explanation: Cell division is the process by which a parent cell divides to form daughter cells; it is important for growth, repair, reproduction and continuity of life.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is mitosis?

options.A: A type of nuclear division that produces four haploid cells
options.B: A type of nuclear division that normally produces two genetically similar daughter nuclei with the same chromosome number as the parent nucleus

questions.explanation: Mitosis is a type of nuclear division that normally produces two genetically similar daughter nuclei with the same chromosome number as the parent nucleus; it supports growth and tissue repair.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are the main stages of mitosis in order?

options.A: Prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase
options.B: Metaphase, prophase, telophase, anaphase

questions.explanation: The main stages of mitosis are prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase, followed by or coordinated with cytokinesis; some texts include prometaphase separately.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What happens during metaphase of mitosis?

options.A: Sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles
options.B: Chromosomes align at the cell's equatorial plane, attached to spindle fibres through kinetochores

questions.explanation: During metaphase of mitosis, chromosomes align at the cell's equatorial plane, attached to spindle fibres through kinetochores.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What happens during anaphase of mitosis?

options.A: Chromosomes align at the equator
options.B: Sister chromatids separate and move towards opposite poles of the cell

questions.explanation: During anaphase of mitosis, sister chromatids separate and move towards opposite poles of the cell.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is cytokinesis?

options.A: Division of the nucleus
options.B: Division of the cytoplasm to form separate daughter cells

questions.explanation: Cytokinesis is the division of the cytoplasm to form separate daughter cells; it follows or overlaps the end of nuclear division.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is meiosis?

options.A: A type of nuclear division that produces two identical cells
options.B: A specialised cell division involving two successive divisions that usually produces four haploid cells

questions.explanation: Meiosis is a specialised cell division involving two successive divisions that usually produces four haploid cells from one diploid cell; it reduces chromosome number and creates genetic variation.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the difference between mitosis and meiosis?

options.A: Mitosis produces four haploid cells; meiosis produces two diploid cells
options.B: Mitosis generally produces two genetically similar cells with unchanged chromosome number; meiosis generally produces four genetically varied haploid cells and halves chromosome number
options.C: Mitosis occurs only in gametes; meiosis occurs in somatic cells
options.D: Mitosis involves crossing over; meiosis does not

questions.explanation: Mitosis generally produces two genetically similar cells with unchanged chromosome number; meiosis generally produces four genetically varied haploid cells and halves chromosome number.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: During which stage does crossing over occur?

options.A: Prophase I of meiosis
options.B: Metaphase of mitosis

questions.explanation: Crossing over occurs during prophase I of meiosis, when homologous chromosomes pair and exchange corresponding DNA segments.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a stem cell?

options.A: An undifferentiated or partially differentiated cell capable of self-renewal and differentiation
options.B: A cell that has lost the ability to divide
options.D: A cell that is specialised for contraction

questions.explanation: A stem cell is an undifferentiated or partially differentiated cell capable of self-renewal and differentiation into one or more specialised cell types.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are embryonic stem cells?

options.A: Pluripotent cells from early embryos that can give rise to nearly all body cell types
options.B: Tissue-specific stem cells found in developed tissues
options.C: Cells found only in bone marrow

questions.explanation: Embryonic stem cells are pluripotent cells from early embryos that can give rise to nearly all body cell types.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are adult stem cells?

options.A: Pluripotent cells from early embryos
options.B: Tissue-specific stem cells found in developed tissues with more limited differentiation potential
options.C: Cells that can form any cell type in the body

questions.explanation: Adult stem cells are tissue-specific stem cells found in developed tissues, such as blood-forming stem cells in bone marrow; they generally have more limited differentiation potential than embryonic stem cells.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the main function of the digestive system?

options.A: To pump blood throughout the body
options.B: To ingest food, break it down, absorb nutrients and water, and eliminate undigested material
options.C: To exchange gases with the environment
options.D: To filter waste from the blood

questions.explanation: The digestive system's main function is to ingest food, mechanically and chemically break it down, absorb nutrients and water, and eliminate undigested material.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the correct pathway of food through the alimentary canal?

options.A: Mouth → oesophagus → pharynx → stomach → small intestine → large intestine → rectum → anus
options.B: Mouth → pharynx → oesophagus → stomach → small intestine → large intestine → rectum → anus
options.C: Mouth → stomach → oesophagus → small intestine → large intestine → rectum → anus
options.D: Mouth → pharynx → stomach → oesophagus → large intestine → small intestine → rectum → anus

questions.explanation: The pathway of food through the alimentary canal is: Mouth → pharynx → oesophagus → stomach → small intestine → large intestine → rectum → anus.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How many permanent teeth does a typical adult have?
questions.explanation: A typical adult usually has 32 permanent teeth, including four third molars (wisdom teeth); some people have fewer because wisdom teeth may be absent or removed.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the function of saliva?

options.A: It digests proteins
options.B: It moistens and lubricates food, helps swallowing, buffers acids and begins starch digestion through salivary amylase

questions.explanation: Saliva moistens and lubricates food, helps swallowing, buffers acids and begins starch digestion through salivary amylase.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which are the three major pairs of salivary glands?

options.A: Parotid, submandibular and sublingual glands
options.B: Parathyroid, thyroid and adrenal glands

questions.explanation: The three major pairs of salivary glands are parotid, submandibular (submaxillary) and sublingual glands.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is peristalsis?

options.A: The breakdown of food by enzymes
options.B: Wave-like contraction and relaxation of smooth muscle that moves food through the digestive tract
options.C: The absorption of nutrients in the small intestine

questions.explanation: Peristalsis is wave-like contraction and relaxation of smooth muscle that moves food through the digestive tract.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which enzyme in the stomach digests proteins?

options.A: Amylase
options.B: Pepsin

questions.explanation: Pepsin digests proteins in the stomach; it is secreted as inactive pepsinogen and activated in the acidic stomach environment.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the function of hydrochloric acid in the stomach?

options.A: It digests carbohydrates
options.B: It creates an acidic environment, helps activate pepsinogen and helps kill many ingested microorganisms

questions.explanation: Hydrochloric acid creates an acidic environment, helps activate pepsinogen and helps kill many ingested microorganisms.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Where does most digestion and nutrient absorption occur?

options.A: Stomach
options.B: Small intestine

questions.explanation: Most digestion and nutrient absorption occur in the small intestine, especially the duodenum, jejunum and ileum.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are the three parts of the small intestine?

options.A: Duodenum, jejunum and ileum
options.B: Caecum, colon and rectum

questions.explanation: The three parts of the small intestine are the duodenum, jejunum and ileum.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are villi and microvilli?

options.A: Finger-like projections that increase surface area for absorption in the small intestine
options.B: Structures that produce digestive enzymes in the stomach

questions.explanation: Villi are finger-like projections of the small-intestinal lining; microvilli are microscopic projections on epithelial cells. Both increase surface area for absorption.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the main function of the large intestine?

options.A: Digestion of proteins
options.B: Absorption of water and electrolytes, processing of intestinal contents and formation of faeces

questions.explanation: The main function of the large intestine is absorption of water and electrolytes, processing of intestinal contents by gut microbes and formation/storage of faeces.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the function of bile?

options.A: It digests proteins
options.B: It emulsifies fats

questions.explanation: Bile is produced by the liver, stored and concentrated in the gallbladder, and released into the duodenum; bile salts emulsify fats but are not digestive enzymes.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Where is bile stored?

options.A: Liver
options.B: Gallbladder

questions.explanation: Bile is produced by the liver, stored and concentrated in the gallbladder, and released into the duodenum.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the function of the pancreas in digestion?

options.A: It produces bile
options.B: Its exocrine part releases digestive enzymes and bicarbonate into the duodenum

questions.explanation: The exocrine part of the pancreas releases digestive enzymes and bicarbonate into the duodenum; its endocrine part releases hormones including insulin and glucagon.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which enzyme breaks down starch into smaller carbohydrates?

options.A: Protease
options.B: Lipase

questions.explanation: Amylase breaks starch into smaller carbohydrates; proteases such as pepsin and trypsin break proteins; lipases break triglycerides.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the main function of the respiratory system?

options.A: To digest food
options.B: To bring oxygen into the body and remove carbon dioxide through gas exchange

questions.explanation: The main function of the respiratory system is to bring oxygen into the body and remove carbon dioxide through gas exchange between air and blood.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the correct pathway of air into the lungs?

options.A: Nose → pharynx → larynx → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli
options.B: Nose → trachea → pharynx → larynx → bronchi → alveoli
options.C: Nose → larynx → pharynx → trachea → alveoli → bronchi

questions.explanation: The pathway of air into the lungs is: Nose/nasal cavity → pharynx → larynx → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the function of the nasal cavity?

options.A: It produces sound
options.B: It filters, warms and moistens inhaled air and contains olfactory receptors

questions.explanation: The nasal cavity filters, warms and moistens inhaled air and contains olfactory receptors for smell.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the function of the trachea?

options.A: It exchanges gases
options.B: It conducts air to the bronchi and is supported by C-shaped cartilage rings

questions.explanation: The trachea conducts air to the bronchi and is supported by C-shaped cartilage rings that help keep it open.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are alveoli?

options.A: Large airways in the lungs
options.B: Tiny thin-walled air sacs surrounded by capillaries where gas exchange occurs

questions.explanation: Alveoli are tiny thin-walled air sacs surrounded by capillaries where oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged by diffusion.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How does inhalation occur?

options.A: The diaphragm relaxes and the ribs move down
options.B: The diaphragm contracts and flattens, external intercostal muscles raise the ribs, thoracic volume increases, lung pressure falls and air flows in
options.C: The lungs actively expand by themselves
options.D: The trachea contracts to pull air in

questions.explanation: During inhalation, the diaphragm contracts and flattens, external intercostal muscles raise the ribs, thoracic volume increases, lung pressure falls and air flows in.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How does gas exchange occur in the alveoli?

options.A: By active transport
options.B: Oxygen diffuses from alveolar air into blood, while carbon dioxide diffuses from blood into alveoli, down their partial-pressure gradients

questions.explanation: Gas exchange in the alveoli occurs by diffusion: oxygen diffuses from alveolar air into blood, while carbon dioxide diffuses from blood into alveoli, down their partial-pressure gradients.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How is most oxygen transported in human blood?

options.A: Dissolved in plasma
options.B: Bound reversibly to haemoglobin in red blood cells as oxyhaemoglobin

questions.explanation: Most oxygen is transported bound reversibly to haemoglobin in red blood cells as oxyhaemoglobin; a small amount is dissolved in plasma.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How is most carbon dioxide transported in blood?

options.A: As oxyhaemoglobin
options.B: Mainly as bicarbonate ions in plasma, with smaller amounts bound to haemoglobin or dissolved in plasma

questions.explanation: Most carbon dioxide is transported mainly as bicarbonate ions in plasma, with smaller amounts bound to haemoglobin or dissolved in plasma.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is cellular respiration?

options.A: The process of breathing
options.B: The set of biochemical processes by which cells release energy from nutrients and capture some of it in ATP
options.C: The exchange of gases in the lungs
options.D: The transport of oxygen in blood

questions.explanation: Cellular respiration is the set of biochemical processes by which cells release energy from nutrients and capture some of it in ATP.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is anaerobic respiration or fermentation?

options.A: Respiration that uses oxygen as the final electron acceptor
options.B: Energy-yielding pathways that operate without oxygen
options.C: The exchange of gases in alveoli
options.D: The transport of oxygen by haemoglobin

questions.explanation: Anaerobic respiration or fermentation refers to energy-yielding pathways that operate without oxygen; in human muscle, glucose breakdown can produce lactate, while yeast fermentation produces ethanol and carbon dioxide.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are the main components of blood?

options.A: Plasma, red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets
options.B: Plasma and platelets only
options.C: Red blood cells and white blood cells only

questions.explanation: The main components of blood are plasma, red blood cells (erythrocytes), white blood cells (leukocytes) and platelets (thrombocytes).

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is plasma?

options.A: The liquid component of blood, consisting mainly of water and containing proteins, electrolytes, nutrients, hormones, gases and waste products
options.B: The solid component of blood
options.C: A type of white blood cell
options.D: A cell fragment that helps clotting

questions.explanation: Plasma is the liquid component of blood, consisting mainly of water and containing proteins, electrolytes, nutrients, hormones, gases and waste products.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the main function of red blood cells?

options.A: Defence against infection
options.B: Transport of oxygen using haemoglobin and contribution to carbon dioxide transport

questions.explanation: The main function of red blood cells is transport of oxygen using haemoglobin and contribution to carbon dioxide transport; mature human red blood cells lack a nucleus.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is haemoglobin?

options.A: An iron-containing protein in red blood cells that binds oxygen reversibly
options.B: A digestive enzyme
options.C: A hormone produced by the thyroid
options.D: A type of white blood cell

questions.explanation: Haemoglobin is an iron-containing protein in red blood cells that binds oxygen reversibly and gives blood its red colour.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the main function of white blood cells?

options.A: Transport of oxygen
options.B: Defence against infection and other foreign substances

questions.explanation: The main function of white blood cells is defence against infection and other foreign substances; different types perform phagocytosis, antibody production and cell-mediated immune functions.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are platelets?

options.A: Small cell fragments derived from megakaryocytes that help form platelet plugs and initiate blood clotting
options.B: Mature red blood cells
options.C: A type of white blood cell

questions.explanation: Platelets are small cell fragments derived from megakaryocytes that help form platelet plugs and initiate blood clotting.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are the main ABO blood groups?

options.A: A, B, AB and O
options.B: A, B and C

questions.explanation: The main ABO blood groups are A, B, AB and O, determined by the presence or absence of A and B antigens on red blood cells.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which antibodies are normally present in the plasma of a person with blood group A?

options.A: Anti-A
options.B: Anti-B

questions.explanation: Group A has anti-B antibodies; group B has anti-A; group AB has neither; group O has both anti-A and anti-B.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which ABO/Rh group is often called the universal red-cell recipient?

options.A: O negative
options.B: AB positive

questions.explanation: AB positive is commonly described as the universal red-cell recipient, but proper compatibility testing remains necessary.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the Rh factor?

options.A: A blood-group system where the D antigen is the most clinically important
options.B: A type of white blood cell
options.D: A hormone produced by the kidneys

questions.explanation: The Rh factor is a blood-group system; the D antigen is the most clinically important. People with the D antigen are usually called Rh-positive and those without it Rh-negative.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which vitamin is important for normal synthesis of several clotting factors?

options.A: Vitamin A
options.B: Vitamin C

questions.explanation: Vitamin K is important for the activation of several blood-clotting proteins and also contributes to bone metabolism.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are the four chambers of the human heart?

options.A: Right atrium, right ventricle, left atrium and left ventricle
options.B: Right atrium, left atrium, aorta and vena cava
options.C: Right ventricle, left ventricle, pulmonary artery and aorta

questions.explanation: The four chambers of the human heart are the right atrium, right ventricle, left atrium and left ventricle.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which side of the heart pumps blood to the lungs?

options.A: The left side
options.B: The right side; the right ventricle sends deoxygenated blood through the pulmonary artery to the lungs

questions.explanation: The right side of the heart pumps blood to the lungs; the right ventricle sends deoxygenated blood through the pulmonary artery to the lungs.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which side of the heart pumps blood to the body?

options.A: The right side
options.B: The left side; the left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood through the aorta to the systemic circulation

questions.explanation: The left side of the heart pumps blood to the body; the left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood through the aorta to the systemic circulation.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the normal route of blood through the heart?

options.A: Body → venae cavae → right atrium → tricuspid valve → right ventricle → pulmonary valve → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary veins → left atrium → mitral valve → left ventricle → aortic valve → aorta → body
options.B: Body → aorta → left atrium → mitral valve → left ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary veins → right atrium → tricuspid valve → right ventricle → venae cavae → body
options.C: Lungs → pulmonary veins → right atrium → tricuspid valve → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → body
options.D: Body → venae cavae → left atrium → mitral valve → left ventricle → aorta → body

questions.explanation: The normal route of blood through the heart is: Body → venae cavae → right atrium → tricuspid valve → right ventricle → pulmonary valve → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary veins → left atrium → mitral valve → left ventricle → aortic valve → aorta → body.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are arteries?

options.A: Blood vessels that carry blood towards the heart
options.B: Blood vessels that carry blood away from the heart; they usually have thick, elastic, muscular walls

questions.explanation: Arteries are blood vessels that carry blood away from the heart; they usually have thick, elastic, muscular walls. Pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are veins?

options.A: Blood vessels that carry blood away from the heart
options.B: Blood vessels that carry blood towards the heart; many contain valves
options.C: Microscopic vessels with very thin walls
options.D: Vessels that carry only oxygenated blood

questions.explanation: Veins are blood vessels that carry blood towards the heart; many contain valves. Pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are capillaries?

options.A: Large vessels that carry blood away from the heart
options.B: Microscopic vessels with very thin walls where gases, nutrients and wastes are exchanged between blood and tissues
options.D: Vessels that carry only deoxygenated blood

questions.explanation: Capillaries are microscopic vessels with very thin walls where gases, nutrients and wastes are exchanged between blood and tissues.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is pulmonary circulation?

options.A: Flow of blood from the left ventricle to body tissues
options.B: Flow of blood from the right ventricle to the lungs and back to the left atrium
options.C: Flow of blood within the heart chambers only
options.D: Flow of blood from the body to the right atrium only

questions.explanation: Pulmonary circulation is the flow of blood from the right ventricle to the lungs and back to the left atrium.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is systemic circulation?

options.A: Flow of blood from the right ventricle to the lungs
options.B: Flow of blood from the left ventricle to body tissues and back to the right atrium
options.C: Flow of blood within the heart only

questions.explanation: Systemic circulation is the flow of blood from the left ventricle to body tissues and back to the right atrium.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is double circulation?

options.A: Blood passes through the heart once in one complete circuit
options.B: The human circulatory system passes blood through the heart twice in one complete circuit: once through pulmonary circulation and once through systemic circulation
options.C: Blood flows in two directions simultaneously

questions.explanation: Double circulation means the human circulatory system passes blood through the heart twice in one complete circuit: once through pulmonary circulation and once through systemic circulation.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is blood pressure?

options.A: The number of heartbeats per minute
options.B: The force exerted by circulating blood on vessel walls
options.C: The volume of blood in the body

questions.explanation: Blood pressure is the force exerted by circulating blood on vessel walls; systemic arterial pressure is commonly recorded as systolic over diastolic pressure in mmHg.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the lymphatic system?

options.A: A network of vessels that carries blood away from the heart
options.B: A network of lymph vessels, nodes and organs that returns tissue fluid to the blood, absorbs dietary fats and supports immune defence
options.C: The system that produces red blood cells only

questions.explanation: The lymphatic system is a network of lymph vessels, nodes and organs that returns tissue fluid to the blood, absorbs dietary fats from the intestine and supports immune defence.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are the main organs of the urinary system?

options.A: Two kidneys, two ureters, urinary bladder and urethra
options.B: Liver, gallbladder and pancreas

questions.explanation: The main organs of the urinary system are two kidneys, two ureters, urinary bladder and urethra.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the function of the kidneys?

options.A: They digest food
options.B: They filter blood, remove metabolic wastes, regulate water and electrolyte balance, help control acid-base balance and blood pressure, and produce hormones such as erythropoietin

questions.explanation: The kidneys filter blood, remove metabolic wastes, regulate water and electrolyte balance, help control acid-base balance and blood pressure, and produce hormones such as erythropoietin.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a nephron?

options.A: The structural and functional unit of the kidney
options.B: A type of white blood cell
options.D: The functional unit of the lungs

questions.explanation: A nephron is the structural and functional unit of the kidney; it includes a renal corpuscle (glomerulus and Bowman's capsule) and a renal tubule.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How is urine formed?

options.A: By simple filtration only
options.B: By glomerular filtration, selective tubular reabsorption and tubular secretion
options.C: By active transport in the bladder

questions.explanation: Urine is formed by glomerular filtration, selective tubular reabsorption and tubular secretion; the resulting urine passes through collecting ducts to the renal pelvis and ureter.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the function of the ureters?

options.A: They store urine
options.B: They carry urine from each kidney to the urinary bladder by peristaltic contractions

questions.explanation: The ureters carry urine from each kidney to the urinary bladder by peristaltic contractions.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the function of the urinary bladder?

options.A: It filters blood
options.B: It temporarily stores urine until urination
options.C: It carries urine to the outside

questions.explanation: The urinary bladder temporarily stores urine until urination.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the function of the urethra?

options.A: It filters blood
options.B: It carries urine from the bladder to the outside of the body
options.D: It carries urine from the kidney to the bladder

questions.explanation: The urethra carries urine from the bladder to the outside of the body; in males it also carries semen, but not at the same time as urination.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the difference between excretion and egestion?

options.A: Excretion is removal of undigested food; egestion is removal of metabolic waste
options.B: Excretion is removal of metabolic waste products; egestion is removal of undigested food
options.D: Excretion occurs only in plants; egestion only in animals

questions.explanation: Excretion is removal of metabolic waste products and excess substances from the body; it is distinct from egestion, which is removal of undigested food.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is dialysis?

options.A: A treatment that removes waste products and excess fluid from blood when kidney function is severely impaired
options.B: A type of blood transfusion
options.C: A surgical procedure to remove the kidney
options.D: A method of measuring blood pressure

questions.explanation: Dialysis is a treatment that removes waste products and excess fluid from blood when kidney function is severely impaired; haemodialysis uses an external filter and peritoneal dialysis uses the peritoneal membrane.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the central nervous system?

options.A: All nerves outside the brain and spinal cord
options.B: The brain and spinal cord

questions.explanation: The central nervous system consists of the brain and spinal cord; it receives, processes and coordinates information and responses.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are the main parts of the brain?

options.A: Cerebrum, diencephalon, brainstem and cerebellum
options.B: Cerebrum and spinal cord only

questions.explanation: The main parts of the brain are the cerebrum, diencephalon (including thalamus and hypothalamus), brainstem (midbrain, pons and medulla oblongata) and cerebellum.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are major functions of the cerebrum?

options.A: Coordination of movement and balance
options.B: Conscious thought, memory, language, sensory interpretation, voluntary movement and higher cognitive functions
options.C: Regulation of breathing and heart rate

questions.explanation: Major functions of the cerebrum include conscious thought, memory, language, sensory interpretation, voluntary movement and higher cognitive functions.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the function of the cerebellum?

options.A: Regulation of breathing
options.B: Coordination of movement, balance, posture and motor learning

questions.explanation: The cerebellum coordinates movement, balance, posture and motor learning.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the function of the medulla oblongata?

options.A: It contains vital centres involved in regulating breathing, heart rate, blood pressure and reflexes such as swallowing and coughing
options.B: It controls conscious thought

questions.explanation: The medulla oblongata contains vital centres involved in regulating breathing, heart rate, blood pressure and reflexes such as swallowing and coughing.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the function of the hypothalamus?

options.A: It coordinates movement
options.B: It helps regulate temperature, hunger, thirst, circadian rhythms, autonomic functions and pituitary hormone control
options.C: It is the centre for conscious thought

questions.explanation: The hypothalamus helps regulate temperature, hunger, thirst, circadian rhythms, autonomic functions and pituitary hormone control.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the function of the spinal cord?

options.A: It produces hormones
options.B: It transmits signals between the brain and body and coordinates many reflex actions

questions.explanation: The spinal cord transmits signals between the brain and body and coordinates many reflex actions.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the peripheral nervous system?

options.A: The brain and spinal cord
options.B: All nerves and ganglia outside the brain and spinal cord

questions.explanation: The peripheral nervous system includes all nerves and ganglia outside the brain and spinal cord; it connects the central nervous system with the rest of the body.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are the main parts of a neuron?

options.A: Cell body (soma), dendrites and axon
options.B: Nucleus, mitochondria and ribosomes

questions.explanation: The main parts of a neuron are the cell body (soma), dendrites and axon; many axons are covered by a myelin sheath.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a nerve impulse?

options.A: A chemical signal released into the blood
options.B: An electrical signal, usually an action potential, produced by changes in membrane ion permeability and propagated along a neuron
options.C: A hormone secreted by a gland

questions.explanation: A nerve impulse is an electrical signal, usually an action potential, produced by changes in membrane ion permeability and propagated along a neuron.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a synapse?

options.A: A junction where a neuron communicates with another neuron or target cell
options.B: The cell body of a neuron
options.C: The myelin sheath around an axon

questions.explanation: A synapse is a junction where a neuron communicates with another neuron or target cell, commonly through chemical neurotransmitters.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a reflex action?

options.A: A conscious, voluntary response to a stimulus
options.B: A rapid, automatic response to a stimulus that occurs through a reflex pathway without requiring conscious initiation

questions.explanation: A reflex action is a rapid, automatic response to a stimulus that occurs through a reflex pathway without requiring conscious initiation.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the pathway of a reflex arc?

options.A: Receptor → sensory neuron → integration centre → motor neuron → effector
options.B: Effector → motor neuron → integration centre → sensory neuron → receptor
options.C: Receptor → motor neuron → integration centre → sensory neuron → effector

questions.explanation: The pathway of a reflex arc is: receptor → sensory neuron → integration centre (often spinal cord) → motor neuron → effector.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the difference between sensory and motor nerves?

options.A: Sensory pathways carry commands from the CNS; motor pathways carry information towards the CNS
options.B: Sensory (afferent) pathways carry information towards the central nervous system; motor (efferent) pathways carry commands from it to muscles or glands
options.C: Sensory nerves are only found in the brain; motor nerves are only found in the spinal cord

questions.explanation: Sensory (afferent) pathways carry information towards the central nervous system; motor (efferent) pathways carry commands from it to muscles or glands.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the autonomic nervous system?

options.A: The part of the peripheral nervous system that regulates involuntary functions of organs, smooth muscle, cardiac muscle and glands
options.B: The part of the nervous system that controls voluntary movement

questions.explanation: The autonomic nervous system is the part of the peripheral nervous system that regulates involuntary functions of organs, smooth muscle, cardiac muscle and glands.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the sympathetic nervous system?

options.A: A division of the autonomic nervous system that generally prepares the body for fight or flight
options.B: A division that supports rest and digest functions

questions.explanation: The sympathetic nervous system generally prepares the body for fight or flight, increasing alertness and mobilising energy.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the parasympathetic nervous system?

options.A: A division that prepares the body for fight or flight
options.B: A division of the autonomic nervous system that generally supports rest and digest functions

questions.explanation: The parasympathetic nervous system generally supports rest and digest functions, such as digestion and energy conservation.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is an endocrine gland?

options.A: A gland with ducts that releases substances to the surface
options.B: A ductless gland that releases hormones into the blood or surrounding fluid
options.D: A part of the digestive system

questions.explanation: An endocrine gland is a ductless gland that releases hormones into the blood or surrounding fluid to act on target cells.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a hormone?

options.A: A chemical messenger produced by endocrine cells that regulates activity in target cells
options.B: A digestive enzyme

questions.explanation: A hormone is a chemical messenger produced by endocrine cells that regulates activity in target cells with appropriate receptors.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which gland is often called the master gland?

options.A: Thyroid gland
options.B: Pituitary gland

questions.explanation: The pituitary gland is often called the master gland because its hormones regulate several other endocrine glands; however, it is itself controlled in large part by the hypothalamus.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is growth hormone?

options.A: A pituitary hormone that supports body growth, protein synthesis and metabolism
options.B: A thyroid hormone that regulates metabolism
options.C: A pancreatic hormone that lowers blood glucose
options.D: An adrenal hormone involved in stress response

questions.explanation: Growth hormone is a pituitary hormone that supports body growth, protein synthesis and metabolism; excess or deficiency during childhood can alter growth.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the function of the thyroid gland?

options.A: It produces insulin
options.B: It produces thyroid hormones that regulate metabolic rate, growth and development, and calcitonin

questions.explanation: The thyroid gland produces thyroid hormones (mainly T3 and T4) that regulate metabolic rate, growth and development; it also produces calcitonin.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is thyroxine?

options.A: A pancreatic hormone
options.B: A thyroid hormone containing iodine that helps regulate metabolism

questions.explanation: Thyroxine (T4) is a thyroid hormone containing iodine; it is converted in tissues to the more active T3 and helps regulate metabolism.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the function of the parathyroid glands?

options.A: They secrete insulin
options.B: They secrete parathyroid hormone (PTH), which raises blood calcium

questions.explanation: The parathyroid glands secrete parathyroid hormone (PTH), which raises blood calcium through effects on bone, kidneys and vitamin D activation.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are the adrenal glands?

options.A: Glands located in the neck
options.B: Endocrine glands above the kidneys that produce steroid hormones and adrenaline

questions.explanation: The adrenal glands are endocrine glands above the kidneys; the cortex produces steroid hormones such as cortisol and aldosterone, while the medulla produces adrenaline and noradrenaline.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is adrenaline?

options.A: A hormone released mainly by the adrenal medulla during stress that increases heart rate and energy availability
options.B: A thyroid hormone

questions.explanation: Adrenaline is a hormone and neurotransmitter released mainly by the adrenal medulla during stress; it increases heart rate, cardiac output and availability of energy.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is insulin?

options.A: A hormone from pancreatic beta cells that lowers blood glucose
options.B: A hormone from pancreatic alpha cells that raises blood glucose

questions.explanation: Insulin is a hormone from pancreatic beta cells that lowers blood glucose by promoting glucose uptake in certain tissues and storage as glycogen and fat.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is glucagon?

options.A: A hormone from pancreatic beta cells that lowers blood glucose
options.B: A hormone from pancreatic alpha cells that raises blood glucose

questions.explanation: Glucagon is a hormone from pancreatic alpha cells that raises blood glucose, mainly by stimulating liver glycogen breakdown and glucose production.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are gonads?

options.A: The testes in males and ovaries in females that produce gametes and sex hormones
options.B: Endocrine glands in the brain

questions.explanation: Gonads are the testes in males and ovaries in females; they produce gametes and sex hormones.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are the main human sex hormones?

options.A: Insulin and glucagon
options.B: Testosterone, oestrogens and progesterone

questions.explanation: The main human sex hormones include testosterone (testes) and oestrogens and progesterone (ovaries); pituitary hormones FSH and LH regulate gonadal function.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is diabetes mellitus?

options.A: A condition of low blood glucose
options.B: A group of disorders characterised by chronic high blood glucose due to inadequate insulin secretion, impaired insulin action or both

questions.explanation: Diabetes mellitus is a group of disorders characterised by chronic high blood glucose due to inadequate insulin secretion, impaired insulin action or both.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is hypothyroidism?

options.A: A condition in which thyroid hormone production or action is insufficient
options.B: A condition of excessive thyroid hormone
options.D: A condition of high blood calcium

questions.explanation: Hypothyroidism is a condition in which thyroid hormone production or action is insufficient; it can cause fatigue, cold intolerance and slowed metabolism.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is hyperthyroidism?

options.A: A condition of insufficient thyroid hormone
options.B: A condition in which thyroid hormone levels or action are excessive
options.C: A condition of low blood glucose
options.D: A condition of high blood calcium

questions.explanation: Hyperthyroidism is a condition in which thyroid hormone levels or action are excessive; it can cause weight loss, heat intolerance, tremor and rapid heartbeat.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is goitre?

options.A: Abnormal enlargement of the thyroid gland
options.B: Enlargement of the liver

questions.explanation: Goitre is abnormal enlargement of the thyroid gland; iodine deficiency is one cause, but autoimmune and other thyroid disorders can also cause it.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How many bones are usually present in an adult human skeleton?
questions.explanation: A typical adult human skeleton has 206 bones; the number varies slightly due to anatomical variation and fusion.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the axial skeleton?

options.A: The bones of the upper and lower limbs
options.B: The skull, vertebral column, ribs and sternum that form the central axis of the body
options.C: The bones of the pectoral girdle only
options.D: The bones of the hands and feet

questions.explanation: The axial skeleton includes the skull, vertebral column, ribs and sternum; it forms the central axis of the body.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the appendicular skeleton?

options.A: The skull and vertebral column
options.B: The bones of the upper and lower limbs and the pectoral and pelvic girdles
options.D: The bones of the middle ear

questions.explanation: The appendicular skeleton includes the bones of the upper and lower limbs and the pectoral and pelvic girdles that attach them to the axial skeleton.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are the major types of bones by shape?

options.A: Long, short, flat, irregular and sesamoid bones
options.B: Compact and spongy bones only

questions.explanation: The major types of bones by shape are long, short, flat, irregular and sesamoid bones.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a joint?

options.A: A site where two or more bones or skeletal elements meet
options.B: A type of muscle
options.C: A connective tissue that connects muscle to bone

questions.explanation: A joint is a site where two or more bones or skeletal elements meet; joints may be fibrous, cartilaginous or synovial.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is cartilage?

options.A: A flexible connective tissue that supports structures and reduces friction at joints
options.B: A type of muscle tissue
options.C: A fluid found in blood vessels

questions.explanation: Cartilage is a flexible connective tissue with cells called chondrocytes embedded in an extracellular matrix; it supports structures and reduces friction at joints.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is bone marrow?

options.A: A type of connective tissue that covers bones
options.B: Soft tissue within bone cavities; red marrow produces blood cells, while yellow marrow is rich in fat
options.C: The hard outer layer of bone

questions.explanation: Bone marrow is soft tissue within bone cavities; red marrow produces blood cells, while yellow marrow is rich in fat and can have blood-forming capacity under certain conditions.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are the main functions of the skeleton?

options.A: Digestion, absorption and excretion
options.B: Support, protection, movement, mineral storage and blood-cell production

questions.explanation: The main functions of the skeleton are support, protection, movement, mineral storage (especially calcium and phosphate) and blood-cell production in red marrow.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are the three types of muscle tissue?

options.A: Skeletal, smooth and cardiac muscle
options.B: Voluntary, involuntary and reflex muscle

questions.explanation: The three types of muscle tissue are skeletal, smooth and cardiac muscle.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are skeletal muscles?

options.A: Involuntary, non-striated muscles found in organ walls
options.B: Usually voluntary, striated muscles attached to bones that produce movement, maintain posture and generate heat
options.C: Involuntary, striated muscle found in the heart
options.D: Muscles found only in blood vessels

questions.explanation: Skeletal muscles are usually voluntary, striated muscles attached to bones or other structures; they produce movement, maintain posture and generate heat.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are smooth muscles?

options.A: Voluntary, striated muscles attached to bones
options.B: Involuntary, non-striated muscles found in walls of organs and blood vessels
options.C: Involuntary, striated muscle found only in the heart

questions.explanation: Smooth muscles are involuntary, non-striated muscles found in walls of organs and blood vessels; they move substances and regulate passageways.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is cardiac muscle?

options.A: Voluntary, striated muscle attached to bones
options.B: Involuntary, striated muscle found in the heart
options.C: Involuntary, non-striated muscle found in organ walls

questions.explanation: Cardiac muscle is involuntary, striated muscle found in the heart; it contracts rhythmically to pump blood.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the basic mechanism of skeletal muscle contraction?

options.A: The sliding-filament mechanism, where myosin heads interact with actin filaments powered by ATP and regulated by calcium
options.B: Osmosis of water into muscle cells
options.C: Active transport of sodium ions only

questions.explanation: The basic mechanism of skeletal muscle contraction is the sliding-filament mechanism: myosin heads interact with actin filaments, powered by ATP and regulated by calcium, causing sarcomeres to shorten.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are the main functions of muscles?

options.A: Digestion, absorption and excretion
options.B: Movement, posture, joint stability, movement of substances through organs and heat production
options.D: Gas exchange and blood pressure regulation

questions.explanation: The main functions of muscles are movement, posture, joint stability, movement of substances through organs and heat production.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are the main organs of the male reproductive system?

options.A: Ovaries, fallopian tubes and uterus
options.B: Testes, epididymides, vas deferens, urethra, seminal vesicles, prostate, bulbourethral glands, penis and scrotum

questions.explanation: The main organs of the male reproductive system are testes, epididymides, vas deferens, ejaculatory ducts, urethra, seminal vesicles, prostate, bulbourethral glands, penis and scrotum.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are the main functions of the testes?

options.A: Production of ova and secretion of oestrogen
options.B: Production of sperm in seminiferous tubules and secretion of testosterone by Leydig cells

questions.explanation: The testes produce sperm in seminiferous tubules and secrete testosterone by Leydig cells.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Where do sperm mature and become motile?

options.A: In the testes
options.B: In the epididymis

questions.explanation: Sperm mature and become motile in the epididymis, a coiled duct on the posterior surface of each testis.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is semen?

options.A: A fluid containing sperm and secretions from accessory reproductive glands
options.B: A hormone produced by the testes
options.D: A fluid produced by the kidneys

questions.explanation: Semen is a fluid containing sperm and secretions from accessory reproductive glands, including seminal vesicles and prostate.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are the main organs of the female reproductive system?

options.A: Testes, epididymides and vas deferens
options.B: Ovaries, uterine (fallopian) tubes, uterus, cervix and vagina

questions.explanation: The main organs of the female reproductive system are ovaries, uterine (fallopian) tubes, uterus, cervix and vagina; external genital structures are collectively called the vulva.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are the main functions of the ovaries?

options.A: Production of sperm and secretion of testosterone
options.B: Production of ova (oocytes) and secretion of hormones including oestrogens and progesterone
options.D: Filtration of blood and production of urine

questions.explanation: The main functions of the ovaries are production of ova (oocytes) and secretion of hormones including oestrogens and progesterone.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are gametes?

options.A: Haploid reproductive cells (sperm in males, ovum in females)
options.B: Diploid body cells

questions.explanation: Gametes are haploid reproductive cells; sperm is the male gamete and the ovum (more precisely, the secondary oocyte at ovulation in humans) is the female gamete.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Where does fertilisation usually occur in humans?

options.A: In the uterus
options.B: In the ampulla of the uterine (fallopian) tube

questions.explanation: Fertilisation usually occurs in the ampulla of the uterine (fallopian) tube.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is fertilisation?

options.A: The fusion of the sperm and egg nuclei to form a diploid zygote
options.B: The release of an egg from the ovary
options.C: The implantation of an embryo in the uterus

questions.explanation: Fertilisation is the fusion of the sperm and egg nuclei to form a diploid zygote.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the menstrual cycle?

options.A: A recurring set of ovarian and uterine changes, averaging about 28 days but varying widely
options.B: A single event that occurs only once in a lifetime

questions.explanation: The menstrual cycle is a recurring set of ovarian and uterine changes, averaging about 28 days but varying widely; it includes menstrual, follicular/proliferative, ovulatory and luteal/secretory phases.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which hormones regulate the menstrual cycle?

options.A: Insulin and glucagon
options.B: GnRH, FSH, LH, oestrogen and progesterone

questions.explanation: The menstrual cycle is regulated by GnRH from the hypothalamus, FSH and LH from the pituitary, and ovarian oestrogen and progesterone.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is ovulation?

options.A: The formation of the placenta
options.B: Release of a secondary oocyte from a mature ovarian follicle, usually triggered by an LH surge
options.C: The fusion of sperm and egg
options.D: The shedding of the uterine lining

questions.explanation: Ovulation is the release of a secondary oocyte from a mature ovarian follicle, usually triggered by a surge in luteinising hormone (LH).

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the placenta?

options.A: A temporary organ formed from fetal and maternal tissues that enables exchange of oxygen, nutrients and wastes
options.B: The organ that produces sperm

questions.explanation: The placenta is a temporary organ formed from fetal and maternal tissues that enables exchange of oxygen, nutrients and wastes and produces hormones; maternal and fetal blood normally do not mix directly.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the function of the umbilical cord?

options.A: It connects the fetus to the placenta and contains two umbilical arteries and one umbilical vein
options.B: It produces hormones

questions.explanation: The umbilical cord connects the fetus to the placenta and contains two umbilical arteries and one umbilical vein in the usual arrangement.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is embryonic development?

options.A: The process of childbirth
options.B: The early developmental process after fertilisation, involving cleavage, blastocyst formation, implantation, gastrulation and organ formation
options.D: The formation of the placenta only

questions.explanation: Embryonic development is the early developmental process after fertilisation, involving cleavage, blastocyst formation, implantation, gastrulation and organ formation; later prenatal development is commonly termed fetal development.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is childbirth or parturition?

options.A: The process of fertilisation
options.B: The process of labour and delivery of the baby and placenta, involving coordinated uterine contractions and cervical changes

questions.explanation: Childbirth or parturition is the process of labour and delivery of the baby and placenta, involving coordinated uterine contractions and cervical changes.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is reproductive health?

options.A: A state of physical, mental and social well-being in matters related to the reproductive system
options.B: The absence of any disease
options.C: The ability to produce offspring only
