questions.explanation: Reproductive health is a state of physical, mental and social well-being in matters related to the reproductive system, including informed choices, safe care and prevention/treatment of reproductive disorders.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the function of the eye?

options.A: It detects sound waves
options.B: It detects light and forms visual signals; the cornea and lens focus light on the retina

questions.explanation: The eye detects light and forms visual signals; the cornea and lens focus light on the retina, whose photoreceptors convert light into nerve signals.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are the main parts of the human eye?

options.A: Cornea, iris, pupil, lens, ciliary body, aqueous humour, vitreous humour, retina, choroid, sclera and optic nerve
options.B: Cochlea, semicircular canals, utricle and saccule

questions.explanation: The main parts of the human eye are cornea, iris, pupil, lens, ciliary body, aqueous humour, vitreous humour, retina, choroid, sclera and optic nerve.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the function of the retina?

options.A: It focuses light
options.B: It contains rods and cones that detect light and convert it into neural signals
options.C: It controls the amount of light entering the eye

questions.explanation: The retina contains rods and cones that detect light and convert it into neural signals.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the function of rods and cones?

options.A: Rods are highly sensitive in dim light and support monochromatic vision; cones function best in brighter light and enable colour and high-acuity vision
options.B: Rods enable colour vision; cones function in dim light
options.C: Both rods and cones detect sound waves
options.D: Rods and cones are found in the inner ear

questions.explanation: Rods are highly sensitive in dim light and support monochromatic vision; cones function best in brighter light and enable colour and high-acuity vision.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the blind spot of the eye?

options.A: The optic disc, where the optic nerve exits the retina; it lacks rods and cones
options.B: The centre of the retina

questions.explanation: The blind spot of the eye is the optic disc, where the optic nerve exits the retina; it lacks rods and cones.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the function of the ear?

options.A: It detects light
options.B: It supports hearing and balance

questions.explanation: The ear supports hearing and balance; it includes outer, middle and inner ear structures.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are the three small bones of the middle ear?

options.A: Malleus, incus and stapes
options.B: Cochlea, utricle and saccule

questions.explanation: The three small bones of the middle ear are the malleus, incus and stapes; they transmit and amplify vibrations from the eardrum to the inner ear.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the function of the cochlea?

options.A: It helps maintain balance
options.B: It contains the sensory structures for hearing and converts sound-induced mechanical vibrations into nerve signals

questions.explanation: The cochlea contains the sensory structures for hearing and converts sound-induced mechanical vibrations into nerve signals.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which structures help maintain balance?

options.A: The cochlea only
options.B: The vestibular apparatus of the inner ear, including semicircular canals, utricle and saccule

questions.explanation: The vestibular apparatus of the inner ear, including semicircular canals, utricle and saccule, helps maintain balance.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which cranial nerve carries smell information?

options.A: The olfactory nerve (cranial nerve I)
options.B: The optic nerve (cranial nerve II)

questions.explanation: The olfactory nerve (cranial nerve I) carries smell information.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which cranial nerves carry taste information?

options.A: Olfactory and optic nerves
options.B: Facial (VII), glossopharyngeal (IX) and vagus (X) cranial nerves

questions.explanation: Taste signals travel mainly through facial (VII), glossopharyngeal (IX) and vagus (X) cranial nerves.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are the five traditionally recognised basic taste qualities?

options.A: Sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami
options.B: Sweet, spicy, salty, bitter and sour
options.C: Sweet, sour, pungent, astringent and salty
options.D: Hot, cold, sweet, sour and bitter

questions.explanation: The five traditionally recognised basic taste qualities are sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are the main functions of skin?

options.A: Digestion and absorption
options.B: Protection, temperature regulation, sensation, prevention of water loss, vitamin D synthesis and limited excretion

questions.explanation: The main functions of skin are protection, temperature regulation, sensation, prevention of water loss, vitamin D synthesis initiated by UV exposure and limited excretion through sweat.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is myopia?

options.A: Long-sightedness in which near objects are blurred
options.B: Short-sightedness in which distant objects are blurred; it is commonly corrected with a concave lens

questions.explanation: Myopia is short-sightedness, in which distant objects are blurred; it is commonly corrected with a concave lens.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is hypermetropia?

options.A: Short-sightedness in which distant objects are blurred
options.B: Long-sightedness in which near objects are blurred; it is commonly corrected with a convex lens

questions.explanation: Hypermetropia is long-sightedness, in which near objects are blurred; it is commonly corrected with a convex lens.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is cataract?

options.A: Clouding of the eye's natural lens, causing reduced or blurred vision
options.B: Damage to the optic nerve

questions.explanation: Cataract is clouding of the eye's natural lens, causing reduced or blurred vision.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is glaucoma?

options.A: Clouding of the lens
options.B: A group of eye diseases involving damage to the optic nerve, often associated with raised intraocular pressure

questions.explanation: Glaucoma is a group of eye diseases involving damage to the optic nerve, often associated with raised intraocular pressure but not always.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is colour vision deficiency?

options.A: Reduced ability to distinguish certain colours, commonly due to inherited differences in cone photopigments
options.B: Complete blindness

questions.explanation: Colour vision deficiency is reduced ability to distinguish certain colours, commonly due to inherited differences in cone photopigments.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are the major components of food?

options.A: Carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, water and dietary fibre
options.B: Only carbohydrates and proteins

questions.explanation: The major components of food are carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, water and dietary fibre.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the main function of carbohydrates?

options.A: They are a major energy source; glucose is an important fuel for cells
options.B: They support growth and tissue repair

questions.explanation: Carbohydrates are a major energy source; glucose is an important fuel for cells.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are common sources of carbohydrates?

options.A: Pulses, beans and lentils
options.B: Rice, wheat, maize, millets, potatoes, fruits and sugar

questions.explanation: Common sources of carbohydrates include rice, wheat, maize, millets, potatoes, fruits, sugar and other cereal or starchy foods.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are proteins?

options.A: Macromolecules made of amino acids that support growth, tissue repair and function as enzymes, hormones and antibodies
options.B: Simple sugars

questions.explanation: Proteins are macromolecules made of amino acids; they support growth and tissue repair and function as enzymes, hormones, antibodies, transporters and structural components.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are common sources of protein?

options.A: Rice, wheat and potatoes
options.B: Pulses, beans, lentils, soy, nuts, seeds, milk, eggs, fish and meat

questions.explanation: Common sources of protein include pulses, beans, lentils, soy, nuts, seeds, milk, eggs, fish and meat.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are fats?

options.A: Lipids that provide concentrated energy, form cell membranes, insulate the body and help absorb fat-soluble vitamins
options.B: Proteins that build muscle
options.C: Simple sugars that provide quick energy

questions.explanation: Fats are lipids that provide concentrated energy, form cell membranes, insulate the body and help absorb fat-soluble vitamins.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the energy value of carbohydrates and proteins?

options.A: Approximately 4 kilocalories per gram each
options.B: Approximately 9 kilocalories per gram each

questions.explanation: The energy value of carbohydrates and proteins is approximately 4 kilocalories per gram for each, using common food-energy estimates.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the energy value of fat?

options.A: Approximately 4 kilocalories per gram
options.B: Approximately 7 kilocalories per gram

questions.explanation: The energy value of fat is approximately 9 kilocalories per gram.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are vitamins?

options.A: Organic micronutrients required in small quantities for normal metabolism, growth and health
options.B: Macronutrients required in large quantities

questions.explanation: Vitamins are organic micronutrients required in small quantities for normal metabolism, growth and health; most must be obtained from the diet.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which vitamins are fat-soluble?

options.A: Vitamins A, D, E and K
options.B: Vitamins C and B-complex
options.C: Vitamins A, B, C and D
options.D: Vitamins C, D, E and K

questions.explanation: Vitamins A, D, E and K are fat-soluble vitamins.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which vitamins are water-soluble?

options.A: Vitamins A and D
options.B: Vitamin C and the B-complex vitamins
options.D: Vitamins A, D, E and K

questions.explanation: Vitamin C and the B-complex vitamins are water-soluble vitamins.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the main function of vitamin A?

options.A: It supports vision, epithelial tissue integrity, immune function and normal growth
options.B: It promotes blood clotting

questions.explanation: Vitamin A supports vision, epithelial tissue integrity, immune function and normal growth.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What can vitamin A deficiency cause?

options.A: Scurvy
options.B: Night blindness and, in severe cases, xerophthalmia and corneal damage

questions.explanation: Vitamin A deficiency can cause night blindness and, in severe cases, xerophthalmia and corneal damage.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What can vitamin B1 (thiamine) deficiency cause?

options.A: Pellagra
options.B: Beriberi

questions.explanation: Vitamin B1 (thiamine) deficiency can cause beriberi; severe deficiency can also cause neurological and cardiac problems.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What can vitamin B3 (niacin) deficiency cause?

options.A: Beriberi
options.B: Pellagra, classically associated with dermatitis, diarrhoea and dementia

questions.explanation: Vitamin B3 (niacin) deficiency can cause pellagra, classically associated with dermatitis, diarrhoea and dementia.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What can vitamin B9 (folate) deficiency cause?

options.A: Scurvy
options.B: Megaloblastic anaemia; deficiency during early pregnancy increases the risk of neural tube defects

questions.explanation: Vitamin B9 (folate) deficiency can cause megaloblastic anaemia; deficiency during early pregnancy increases the risk of neural tube defects in the developing fetus.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What can vitamin B12 deficiency cause?

options.A: Scurvy
options.B: Megaloblastic anaemia and neurological problems

questions.explanation: Vitamin B12 deficiency can cause megaloblastic anaemia and neurological problems; it may occur with inadequate intake or impaired absorption.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the main function of vitamin C?

options.A: It is required for collagen synthesis, antioxidant functions and support of normal connective tissue and wound healing
options.B: It promotes blood clotting

questions.explanation: Vitamin C is required for collagen synthesis, antioxidant functions and support of normal connective tissue and wound healing; it also improves non-haem iron absorption.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What can vitamin C deficiency cause?

options.A: Rickets
options.B: Scurvy, characterised by bleeding gums, poor wound healing and other connective-tissue problems

questions.explanation: Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy, characterised by bleeding gums, poor wound healing and other connective-tissue problems.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the main function of vitamin D?

options.A: It promotes calcium and phosphate absorption and supports bone mineralisation and muscle function
options.B: It acts as a lipid-soluble antioxidant
options.C: It is needed for blood clotting

questions.explanation: Vitamin D promotes calcium and phosphate absorption and supports bone mineralisation and muscle function.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What can vitamin D deficiency cause?

options.A: Scurvy in children and beriberi in adults
options.B: Rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults

questions.explanation: Vitamin D deficiency can cause rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults; long-term deficiency can contribute to poor bone health.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the main function of vitamin E?

options.A: It acts as a lipid-soluble antioxidant that protects cell membranes
options.B: It promotes blood clotting

questions.explanation: Vitamin E acts as a lipid-soluble antioxidant that protects cell membranes; severe deficiency is uncommon but can cause neurological and muscular problems.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the main function of vitamin K?

options.A: It is needed for activation of several blood-clotting proteins and contributes to bone metabolism
options.B: It supports vision

questions.explanation: Vitamin K is needed for activation of several blood-clotting proteins and also contributes to bone metabolism.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the function of iron?

options.A: It is essential for haemoglobin, myoglobin and many enzymes; deficiency can cause iron-deficiency anaemia
options.B: It is required to synthesise thyroid hormones
options.C: It supports bone and teeth formation

questions.explanation: Iron is essential for haemoglobin and myoglobin and many enzymes; deficiency can cause iron-deficiency anaemia.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the function of iodine?

options.A: It is essential for haemoglobin synthesis
options.B: It is required to synthesise thyroid hormones; deficiency can cause goitre and impaired brain development

questions.explanation: Iodine is required to synthesise thyroid hormones; deficiency can cause goitre and impaired brain development in the fetus and child.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the function of calcium?

options.A: It supports bones and teeth, muscle contraction, nerve signalling, blood clotting and intracellular signalling
options.B: It is essential for haemoglobin
options.C: It is required for thyroid hormone synthesis

questions.explanation: Calcium supports bones and teeth, muscle contraction, nerve signalling, blood clotting and intracellular signalling.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the function of water in the body?

options.A: It acts as a solvent, transports substances, regulates temperature, supports chemical reactions and maintains blood volume and cell function
options.B: It provides energy
options.C: It is a source of vitamins
options.D: It is a source of protein

questions.explanation: Water acts as a solvent, transports substances, regulates temperature, supports chemical reactions and maintains blood volume and cell function.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is dietary fibre?

options.A: The indigestible or partly fermentable components of plant foods that support bowel function
options.B: A source of protein

questions.explanation: Dietary fibre refers to the indigestible or partly fermentable components of plant foods that support bowel function and can help regulate blood glucose and cholesterol.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a balanced diet?

options.A: A diet providing adequate energy and all essential nutrients in appropriate proportions
options.B: A diet that includes only carbohydrates
options.C: A diet that excludes all fats
options.D: A diet with only proteins and vitamins

questions.explanation: A balanced diet is a diet providing adequate energy and all essential nutrients in appropriate proportions for a person's age, sex, activity, health and life stage.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is malnutrition?

options.A: A broad condition that includes undernutrition, micronutrient deficiencies, overweight and obesity, and imbalances in nutrient intake
options.B: A condition caused only by lack of protein
options.C: A condition caused only by overeating
options.D: A condition caused by lack of vitamins only

questions.explanation: Malnutrition is a broad condition that includes undernutrition, micronutrient deficiencies, overweight and obesity, and imbalances in nutrient intake.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is protein-energy malnutrition?

options.A: A form of overnutrition caused by excessive protein
options.B: A form of undernutrition caused by inadequate energy and protein intake; severe forms include marasmus and kwashiorkor
options.C: A condition caused by lack of vitamins only
options.D: A condition caused by excessive fat intake

questions.explanation: Protein-energy malnutrition is a form of undernutrition caused by inadequate energy and protein intake; severe clinical forms include marasmus and kwashiorkor.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is marasmus?

options.A: Severe energy deficiency causing marked wasting and loss of body fat and muscle, generally without oedema
options.B: A condition with oedema and fatty liver

questions.explanation: Marasmus is severe energy deficiency causing marked wasting and loss of body fat and muscle, generally without the oedema characteristic of kwashiorkor.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is kwashiorkor?

options.A: Severe energy deficiency without oedema
options.B: A severe form of malnutrition classically associated with oedema, fatty liver, skin and hair changes

questions.explanation: Kwashiorkor is a severe form of malnutrition classically associated with oedema, fatty liver, skin and hair changes and other systemic features; it is not explained by protein deficiency alone.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is anaemia?

options.A: A condition in which haemoglobin concentration or red-cell mass is below the expected range
options.B: A condition of high blood glucose

questions.explanation: Anaemia is a condition in which haemoglobin concentration or red-cell mass is below the expected range, reducing oxygen-carrying capacity; iron deficiency is a common cause.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is rickets?

options.A: Defective mineralisation of growing bones in children, commonly due to vitamin D deficiency
options.B: A vitamin C deficiency

questions.explanation: Rickets is defective mineralisation of growing bones in children, commonly due to vitamin D deficiency or problems with calcium/phosphate metabolism.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is scurvy?

options.A: Disease caused by vitamin A deficiency
options.B: Disease caused by vitamin C deficiency
options.C: Disease caused by vitamin D deficiency

questions.explanation: Scurvy is a disease caused by vitamin C deficiency.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is night blindness?

options.A: Difficulty seeing in bright light
options.B: Difficulty seeing in dim light; vitamin A deficiency is an important nutritional cause

questions.explanation: Night blindness is difficulty seeing in dim light; vitamin A deficiency is an important nutritional cause.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is beriberi?

options.A: Disease caused by thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency, affecting nerves and/or the cardiovascular system
options.B: Disease caused by niacin deficiency
options.C: Disease caused by vitamin C deficiency
options.D: Disease caused by vitamin D deficiency

questions.explanation: Beriberi is a disease caused by thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency, affecting nerves and/or the cardiovascular system.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is pellagra?

options.A: Disease caused by thiamine deficiency
options.B: Disease caused by niacin (vitamin B3) deficiency, classically described by dermatitis, diarrhoea and dementia
options.C: Disease caused by vitamin C deficiency
options.D: Disease caused by vitamin A deficiency

questions.explanation: Pellagra is a disease caused by niacin (vitamin B3) deficiency, classically described by the three Ds: dermatitis, diarrhoea and dementia.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is osteoporosis?

options.A: A skeletal disorder characterised by reduced bone strength and increased fracture risk
options.B: A vitamin C deficiency

questions.explanation: Osteoporosis is a skeletal disorder characterised by reduced bone strength and increased fracture risk due to reduced bone mass and altered bone structure.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is obesity?

options.A: A condition of being underweight
options.B: Excessive accumulation of body fat that can impair health

questions.explanation: Obesity is excessive accumulation of body fat that can impair health; body-mass index is a screening measure, not a direct measurement of body fat.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a communicable disease?

options.A: A disease that cannot be transmitted
options.B: A disease caused by an infectious agent that can be transmitted directly or indirectly

questions.explanation: A communicable disease is a disease caused by an infectious agent that can be transmitted directly or indirectly from one host or source to another.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What causes tuberculosis (TB)?

options.A: A virus
options.B: Mycobacterium tuberculosis, a bacterium spread mainly through infectious airborne particles

questions.explanation: Tuberculosis is usually caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, a bacterium spread mainly through infectious airborne particles from a person with pulmonary or laryngeal TB.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are common symptoms of pulmonary tuberculosis?

options.A: Persistent cough, fever, night sweats, weight loss, fatigue and sometimes blood in sputum
options.B: Severe watery diarrhoea

questions.explanation: Common symptoms of pulmonary tuberculosis include persistent cough, fever, night sweats, weight loss, fatigue and sometimes blood in sputum.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What causes leprosy?

options.A: A virus
options.B: Mycobacterium leprae and, less commonly, Mycobacterium lepromatosis

questions.explanation: Leprosy is caused by Mycobacterium leprae and, less commonly, Mycobacterium lepromatosis; it mainly affects skin and peripheral nerves.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What causes typhoid fever?

options.A: Vibrio cholerae
options.B: Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi, usually transmitted through contaminated food or water

questions.explanation: Typhoid fever is caused by Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi, usually transmitted through food or water contaminated by human faeces.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What causes cholera?

options.A: Salmonella Typhi
options.B: Toxigenic strains of Vibrio cholerae transmitted mainly through contaminated water or food

questions.explanation: Cholera is caused by toxigenic strains of Vibrio cholerae transmitted mainly through contaminated water or food; severe watery diarrhoea can cause rapid dehydration.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the key immediate treatment principle for cholera?

options.A: Antibiotics alone
options.B: Rapid rehydration with oral rehydration solution or intravenous fluids when severe

questions.explanation: The key immediate treatment principle for cholera is rapid rehydration with oral rehydration solution or intravenous fluids when severe; antibiotics may be used in selected cases under medical supervision.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What causes diphtheria?

options.A: Toxin-producing strains of Corynebacterium diphtheriae
options.B: Clostridium tetani

questions.explanation: Diphtheria is caused by toxin-producing strains of Corynebacterium diphtheriae; vaccination is the main preventive measure.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What causes tetanus?

options.A: A virus
options.B: Tetanus toxin produced by Clostridium tetani, whose spores enter wounds

questions.explanation: Tetanus is caused by tetanus toxin produced by Clostridium tetani, whose spores enter wounds; it is not usually spread person-to-person.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How is tetanus prevented?

options.A: Routine vaccination with tetanus-toxoid-containing vaccines, appropriate wound care and tetanus immunoglobulin when indicated
options.B: Drinking boiled water

questions.explanation: Tetanus is prevented by routine vaccination with tetanus-toxoid-containing vaccines, appropriate wound care and, for some wounds or incomplete immunisation, tetanus immunoglobulin as indicated.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What causes malaria?

options.A: A virus transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes
options.B: Protozoan parasites of the genus Plasmodium, transmitted by infected female Anopheles mosquitoes

questions.explanation: Malaria is caused by protozoan parasites of the genus Plasmodium, transmitted to humans by infected female Anopheles mosquitoes.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which Plasmodium species causes the greatest burden of severe malaria globally?

options.A: Plasmodium vivax
options.B: Plasmodium falciparum

questions.explanation: Plasmodium falciparum causes the greatest burden of severe malaria globally among the Plasmodium species that cause human malaria.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What causes dengue?

options.A: Plasmodium species transmitted by Anopheles mosquitoes
options.B: Dengue viruses (DENV 1-4), transmitted mainly by infected Aedes mosquitoes

questions.explanation: Dengue is caused by dengue viruses (DENV 1-4), transmitted mainly by infected Aedes mosquitoes, especially Aedes aegypti.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are warning signs of severe dengue?

options.A: Severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, fluid accumulation, mucosal bleeding, lethargy/restlessness, liver enlargement or rising haematocrit with falling platelets
options.B: Mild fever and runny nose

questions.explanation: Warning signs of severe dengue include severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, fluid accumulation, mucosal bleeding, lethargy/restlessness, liver enlargement or rising haematocrit with falling platelets; urgent medical assessment is needed.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What causes chikungunya?

options.A: Chikungunya virus, transmitted mainly by Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes
options.B: Plasmodium species

questions.explanation: Chikungunya is caused by chikungunya virus, transmitted mainly by Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes; severe joint pain is characteristic.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What causes lymphatic filariasis?

options.A: A virus transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes
options.B: Filarial worms, especially Wuchereria bancrofti and Brugia species, transmitted by mosquitoes

questions.explanation: Lymphatic filariasis is caused by filarial worms, especially Wuchereria bancrofti and Brugia species, transmitted by mosquitoes; chronic disease can cause lymphoedema and elephantiasis.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What causes Japanese encephalitis?

options.A: A bacterium transmitted by ticks
options.B: Japanese encephalitis virus, transmitted mainly by Culex mosquitoes

questions.explanation: Japanese encephalitis is caused by Japanese encephalitis virus, transmitted mainly by Culex mosquitoes; pigs and water birds can act as amplifying or reservoir hosts.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What causes rabies?

options.A: A bacterium transmitted by mosquitoes
options.B: Rabies virus and related lyssaviruses, usually transmitted through the saliva of an infected mammal

questions.explanation: Rabies is caused by rabies virus and related lyssaviruses, usually transmitted through the saliva of an infected mammal, commonly by bites.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What causes AIDS?

options.A: A bacterium
options.B: Advanced immune deficiency caused by human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), which infects and depletes CD4 T lymphocytes

questions.explanation: AIDS is advanced immune deficiency caused by human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), which infects and depletes CD4 T lymphocytes.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the difference between HIV and AIDS?

options.A: HIV is the virus; AIDS is the advanced clinical stage of HIV infection defined by severe immune suppression or certain opportunistic illnesses
options.B: HIV is a bacterium; AIDS is a virus
options.D: HIV affects only animals; AIDS affects humans

questions.explanation: HIV is the virus; AIDS is the advanced clinical stage of HIV infection defined by severe immune suppression or certain opportunistic illnesses.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How is HIV transmitted?

options.A: Through casual contact such as hugging or sharing food
options.B: Through specific body fluids including blood, semen, vaginal/rectal fluids and breast milk, via sexual contact, shared contaminated needles, and vertical transmission

questions.explanation: HIV is transmitted through specific body fluids, including blood, semen, vaginal/rectal fluids and breast milk, via sexual contact, shared contaminated needles, and vertical transmission during pregnancy, birth or breastfeeding.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How is HIV NOT transmitted?

options.A: Through unprotected sexual contact
options.B: Through casual contact such as hugging, sharing food, shaking hands, toilet seats or mosquito bites
options.D: From mother to child during pregnancy

questions.explanation: HIV is not transmitted by casual contact such as hugging, sharing food, shaking hands, toilet seats or mosquito bites.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is hepatitis?

options.A: Inflammation of the kidneys
options.B: Inflammation of the liver; it can be caused by hepatitis viruses, alcohol, medicines, toxins or autoimmune disease

questions.explanation: Hepatitis is inflammation of the liver; it can be caused by hepatitis viruses, alcohol, medicines, toxins or autoimmune disease.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which hepatitis viruses are commonly important in public health?

options.A: Hepatitis A, B, C, D and E
options.B: Hepatitis A, B and C only
options.C: Hepatitis B, C and D only

questions.explanation: Hepatitis A, B, C, D and E are commonly important in public health; A and E are commonly faecal-oral, while B, C and D are primarily blood/body-fluid transmitted.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which hepatitis viruses have widely used vaccines?

options.A: Hepatitis A and B
options.B: Hepatitis C and D

questions.explanation: Vaccines are available for hepatitis A and B; hepatitis B vaccination also prevents hepatitis D infection. No widely used routine vaccine is available for hepatitis C.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What causes polio?

options.A: A bacterium
options.B: Poliovirus, an enterovirus transmitted mainly by the faecal-oral route

questions.explanation: Polio is caused by poliovirus, an enterovirus transmitted mainly by the faecal-oral route; it can invade the nervous system and cause paralysis in a small proportion of infections.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What causes measles?

options.A: A bacterium transmitted by mosquitoes
options.B: Measles virus, transmitted through the air; highly contagious

questions.explanation: Measles is caused by measles virus, transmitted through the air and highly contagious; vaccination with measles-containing vaccine is highly effective prevention.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What causes chickenpox?

options.A: A bacterium
options.B: Varicella-zoster virus (VZV); it causes an itchy vesicular rash and can reactivate later as shingles

questions.explanation: Chickenpox is caused by Varicella-zoster virus (VZV); it causes an itchy vesicular rash and can reactivate later as shingles.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What causes influenza?

options.A: A bacterium
options.B: Influenza viruses, mainly types A and B in seasonal human epidemics

questions.explanation: Influenza is caused by influenza viruses, mainly types A and B in seasonal human epidemics; they spread mainly through respiratory particles.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What causes COVID-19?

options.A: A bacterium
options.B: SARS-CoV-2, a coronavirus transmitted mainly through infectious respiratory particles

questions.explanation: COVID-19 is caused by SARS-CoV-2, a coronavirus transmitted mainly through infectious respiratory particles.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What causes kala-azar (visceral leishmaniasis)?

options.A: A virus transmitted by mosquitoes
options.B: Leishmania parasites, especially Leishmania donovani, transmitted by infected female sandflies

questions.explanation: Kala-azar is caused by Leishmania parasites, especially Leishmania donovani in the Indian subcontinent, transmitted by infected female sandflies.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are non-communicable diseases?

options.A: Diseases transmitted from person to person
options.B: Diseases that are not generally transmitted from person to person; many are chronic and arise from genetic, physiological, environmental and behavioural factors

questions.explanation: Non-communicable diseases are not generally transmitted from person to person; many are chronic and arise from genetic, physiological, environmental and behavioural factors.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is hypertension?

options.A: Persistently low blood pressure
options.B: Persistently elevated arterial blood pressure

questions.explanation: Hypertension is persistently elevated arterial blood pressure; diagnosis is based on properly measured readings over time and applicable clinical guidelines.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are cardiovascular diseases?

options.A: Diseases of the heart and blood vessels, including coronary artery disease, heart failure, stroke and peripheral arterial disease
options.B: Diseases of the lungs only
options.D: Diseases of the nervous system only

questions.explanation: Cardiovascular diseases are diseases of the heart and blood vessels, including coronary artery disease, heart failure, stroke and peripheral arterial disease.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a stroke?

options.A: A heart attack
options.B: Sudden brain injury due to interruption of blood supply or bleeding; it is a medical emergency

questions.explanation: A stroke is sudden brain injury due to interruption of blood supply (ischaemic stroke) or bleeding (haemorrhagic stroke); it is a medical emergency.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is cancer?

options.A: A group of diseases involving uncontrolled growth and spread of abnormal cells
options.B: A bacterial infection
options.C: A genetic disorder caused by a single gene

questions.explanation: Cancer is a group of diseases involving uncontrolled growth and spread of abnormal cells, which may invade nearby tissues and metastasise.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is asthma?

options.A: A chronic inflammatory airway disease with variable respiratory symptoms and variable expiratory airflow limitation
options.B: A heart disease

questions.explanation: Asthma is a chronic inflammatory airway disease with variable respiratory symptoms and variable expiratory airflow limitation; triggers can include allergens, infections, smoke and exercise.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are common causes of chronic kidney disease?

options.A: Diabetes and hypertension
options.B: Vitamin deficiencies

questions.explanation: Diabetes and hypertension are major causes of chronic kidney disease; other causes include glomerular diseases, inherited disorders and recurrent kidney injury.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is innate immunity?

options.A: Antigen-specific immunity involving B and T lymphocytes
options.B: The body's rapid, non-specific first-line defence, including physical barriers, phagocytes, natural killer cells, complement and inflammatory responses
options.D: Immunity transferred from mother to child

questions.explanation: Innate immunity is the body's rapid, non-specific first-line defence, including physical barriers, phagocytes, natural killer cells, complement and inflammatory responses.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is acquired or adaptive immunity?

options.A: Non-specific defence present from birth
options.B: Antigen-specific immunity involving B and T lymphocytes, with immunological memory
options.C: Immunity provided by physical barriers only
options.D: Immunity that does not involve memory

questions.explanation: Acquired or adaptive immunity is antigen-specific immunity involving B and T lymphocytes, with immunological memory; it develops after infection or vaccination.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is an antigen?

options.A: A molecule or molecular structure recognised by an antibody, B-cell receptor or T-cell receptor
options.B: A protein made by B cells that binds antigens
options.C: A type of white blood cell
options.D: A hormone produced by the thymus

questions.explanation: An antigen is a molecule or molecular structure recognised by an antibody, B-cell receptor or T-cell receptor; some antigens can trigger an immune response.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is an antibody?

options.A: A molecule that triggers an immune response
options.B: An immunoglobulin protein made by B cells/plasma cells that specifically binds an antigen

questions.explanation: An antibody is an immunoglobulin protein made by B cells/plasma cells that specifically binds an antigen.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a vaccine?

options.A: A biological preparation that safely presents an antigen or genetic instructions for an antigen to the immune system
options.B: An antibiotic used to treat bacterial infections

questions.explanation: A vaccine is a biological preparation that safely presents an antigen or genetic instructions for an antigen to the immune system, generating protective immune responses and memory.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is immunisation?

options.A: The process of becoming protected against a disease, usually through vaccination
options.B: The process of treating a disease with antibiotics
options.C: The process of diagnosing a disease
options.D: The process of isolating infected individuals

questions.explanation: Immunisation is the process of becoming protected against a disease, usually through vaccination or, in some cases, passive transfer of antibodies.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the difference between active and passive immunity?

options.A: Active immunity results from receiving ready-made antibodies; passive immunity results from vaccination
options.B: Active immunity results when a person's immune system produces its own response after infection or vaccination; passive immunity results from receiving ready-made antibodies and is usually temporary
options.C: Active immunity is temporary; passive immunity is long-lasting

questions.explanation: Active immunity results when a person's immune system produces its own response after infection or vaccination; passive immunity results from receiving ready-made antibodies and is usually temporary.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is herd immunity?

options.A: Immunity acquired by an individual after vaccination
options.B: Indirect protection that occurs when enough people in a population are immune to an infection, reducing its spread
options.C: Immunity that occurs only in animals
options.D: Immunity that cannot be achieved through vaccination

questions.explanation: Herd immunity is indirect protection that occurs when enough people in a population are immune to an infection, reducing its spread; the required level depends on the pathogen and population.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is antibiotic resistance?

options.A: The ability of viruses to survive antibiotics
options.B: The ability of bacteria to survive or grow despite an antibiotic that would normally inhibit or kill them
options.C: The ability of the human body to resist antibiotics

questions.explanation: Antibiotic resistance is the ability of bacteria to survive or grow despite an antibiotic that would normally inhibit or kill them; misuse and overuse of antibiotics accelerate selection for resistance.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Do antibiotics treat viral infections?

options.A: Yes, all antibiotics work against viruses
options.B: No. Antibiotics act against bacteria, not viruses
options.D: Yes, if given in high doses

questions.explanation: Antibiotics act against bacteria, not viruses; they should be used only when clinically indicated.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are basic methods of disease prevention?

options.A: Only vaccination
options.B: Vaccination, hand hygiene, safe water and food, sanitation, ventilation, vector control, safer sex, appropriate protective equipment and early diagnosis/treatment

questions.explanation: Basic methods of disease prevention include vaccination, hand hygiene, safe water and food, sanitation, ventilation, vector control, safer sex, appropriate protective equipment and early diagnosis/treatment.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is personal hygiene?

options.A: Practices that maintain cleanliness and reduce infection risk, such as handwashing, safe food handling, oral hygiene and bathing
options.B: The use of antibiotics

questions.explanation: Personal hygiene refers to practices that maintain cleanliness and reduce infection risk, such as handwashing, safe food handling, oral hygiene and appropriate bathing.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is sanitation?

options.A: The use of vaccines
options.B: Safe management of human waste, wastewater and environmental cleanliness to prevent disease
options.D: The treatment of infections with antibiotics

questions.explanation: Sanitation refers to safe management of human waste, wastewater and environmental cleanliness to prevent disease and protect public health.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is public health?

options.A: The treatment of individual patients in hospitals
options.B: The science and practice of protecting and improving the health of populations through prevention, policy, education, surveillance and organised services

questions.explanation: Public health is the science and practice of protecting and improving the health of populations through prevention, policy, education, surveillance and organised services.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is epidemiology?

options.A: The study of individual diseases
options.B: The study of the distribution and determinants of health-related states or events in populations

questions.explanation: Epidemiology is the study of the distribution and determinants of health-related states or events in populations and the application of this study to control health problems.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is incidence?

options.A: The total number of cases at a given time
options.B: The number or rate of new cases of a disease occurring in a population during a specified period
options.C: The proportion of people with a disease over time
options.D: The death rate from a disease

questions.explanation: Incidence is the number or rate of new cases of a disease occurring in a population during a specified period.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is prevalence?

options.A: The number of new cases in a specified period
options.B: The proportion or number of people in a population who have a disease at a particular time or over a specified period
options.C: The death rate from a disease
options.D: The rate of recovery from a disease

questions.explanation: Prevalence is the proportion or number of people in a population who have a disease or condition at a particular time or over a specified period.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is first aid?

options.A: A surgical procedure
options.B: Immediate, temporary assistance given to an ill or injured person until appropriate medical care is available

questions.explanation: First aid is immediate, temporary assistance given to an ill or injured person until appropriate medical care is available.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the first priority in an emergency first-aid situation?

options.A: Administer medication immediately
options.B: Ensure scene safety, assess responsiveness and breathing, call emergency services and provide appropriate life-saving care within one's training
options.D: Give the person food and water

questions.explanation: The first priority in an emergency first-aid situation is to ensure scene safety, assess responsiveness and breathing, call emergency services and provide appropriate life-saving care within one's training.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is CPR?

options.A: A type of antibiotic
options.B: Cardiopulmonary resuscitation, an emergency procedure using chest compressions and rescue breaths to maintain circulation during cardiac arrest

questions.explanation: CPR stands for cardiopulmonary resuscitation, an emergency procedure using chest compressions and, when trained and equipped, rescue breaths to maintain circulation and oxygenation during cardiac arrest.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the purpose of blood donation?

options.A: To collect blood from eligible donors for transfusion to patients
options.B: To diagnose diseases

questions.explanation: The purpose of blood donation is to collect blood from eligible donors for transfusion to patients; donated blood is tested and processed into components where appropriate.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Can all blood groups donate to all recipients?

options.A: Yes, blood groups do not matter
options.B: No. ABO and Rh compatibility and additional testing are essential
options.C: Yes, if the donor is healthy
options.D: Yes, if the blood is fresh

questions.explanation: Not all blood groups can donate to all recipients; ABO and Rh compatibility and additional testing are essential, and transfusion services perform grouping and crossmatching.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is organ donation?

options.A: The voluntary donation of organs or tissues for transplantation to treat patients with organ failure or serious injury
options.B: The sale of organs for profit
options.C: The removal of organs for research without consent

questions.explanation: Organ donation is the voluntary donation of organs or tissues for transplantation to treat patients with organ failure or serious injury; consent and legal procedures apply.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is heredity?

options.A: The study of fossils
options.B: The transmission of biological characteristics from parents to offspring through genetic information

questions.explanation: Heredity is the transmission of biological characteristics from parents to offspring through genetic information.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is variation?

options.A: Differences in characteristics among individuals of a population
options.B: The transmission of traits from parents to offspring

questions.explanation: Variation refers to differences in characteristics among individuals of a population; variation arises from genetic differences, environmental influences and their interaction.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a gene?

options.A: A segment of DNA that contributes to a functional product and can influence inherited traits
options.B: A type of protein

questions.explanation: A gene is a segment of DNA that contributes to a functional product, such as a protein or functional RNA, and can influence inherited traits.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How many chromosomes do humans normally have in most body cells?
questions.explanation: Humans normally have 46 chromosomes arranged in 23 pairs in most body cells; gametes usually have 23 chromosomes.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is DNA?

options.A: A protein that carries genetic information
options.B: Deoxyribonucleic acid, the main hereditary material in humans and most organisms; it usually forms a double helix
options.D: A lipid found in cell membranes

questions.explanation: DNA is deoxyribonucleic acid, the main hereditary material in humans and most organisms; it usually forms a double helix of two complementary nucleotide strands.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are the four bases in DNA?

options.A: Adenine (A), thymine (T), guanine (G) and cytosine (C)
options.B: Adenine (A), uracil (U), guanine (G) and cytosine (C)

questions.explanation: The four bases in DNA are adenine (A), thymine (T), guanine (G) and cytosine (C); A pairs with T and G pairs with C in standard DNA.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is RNA?

options.A: A double-stranded molecule containing thymine
options.B: Ribonucleic acid, usually single-stranded, involved in gene expression and protein synthesis; it contains ribose and uracil instead of thymine
options.C: A protein that carries genetic information
options.D: A lipid found in cell membranes

questions.explanation: RNA is ribonucleic acid, usually single-stranded, involved in gene expression and protein synthesis; it contains ribose and uracil instead of thymine.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are the main types of RNA involved in protein synthesis?

options.A: mRNA, tRNA and rRNA
options.B: DNA, RNA and protein

questions.explanation: The main types of RNA involved in protein synthesis are messenger RNA (mRNA), transfer RNA (tRNA) and ribosomal RNA (rRNA).

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a codon?

options.A: A sequence of three nucleotides in mRNA that specifies an amino acid or a translation stop signal
options.B: A single nucleotide in DNA
options.C: A protein that regulates gene expression

questions.explanation: A codon is a sequence of three nucleotides in mRNA that specifies an amino acid or a translation stop signal.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the start codon in the standard genetic code?

options.A: UAA
options.B: AUG

questions.explanation: AUG is the start codon in the standard genetic code; it codes for methionine and usually initiates translation.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which are the three stop codons in the standard genetic code?

options.A: UAA, UAG and UGA
options.B: AUG, UAA and UAG

questions.explanation: The three stop codons in the standard genetic code are UAA, UAG and UGA.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a dominant allele?

options.A: An allele whose effect is masked in a heterozygote
options.B: An allele whose effect is expressed in a heterozygote in a simple dominance relationship
options.C: An allele that is always more common in a population

questions.explanation: A dominant allele is an allele whose effect is expressed in a heterozygote in a simple dominance relationship; dominance does not necessarily mean more common or stronger.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a recessive allele?

options.A: An allele whose effect is expressed in a heterozygote
options.B: An allele whose phenotype is generally masked by a dominant allele in a heterozygote and expressed in a homozygote
options.C: An allele that is always harmful
options.D: An allele that is always more common

questions.explanation: A recessive allele is an allele whose phenotype is generally masked by a dominant allele in a heterozygote and expressed in a homozygote in simple Mendelian inheritance.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Who is called the father of genetics?

options.A: Charles Darwin
options.B: Gregor Johann Mendel

questions.explanation: Gregor Johann Mendel is called the father of genetics, based on his experiments with pea plants and formulation of inheritance principles.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What organism did Mendel use in his inheritance experiments?

options.A: Fruit fly
options.B: Garden pea (Pisum sativum)

questions.explanation: Mendel used the garden pea, Pisum sativum, in his inheritance experiments.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is Mendel's law of segregation?

options.A: Alleles of different genes assort independently
options.B: The two alleles of a gene separate during gamete formation, so each gamete receives one allele

questions.explanation: Mendel's law of segregation states that the two alleles of a gene separate during gamete formation, so each gamete receives one allele; the pair is restored at fertilisation.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is Mendel's law of independent assortment?

options.A: Alleles of a single gene separate during gamete formation
options.B: Alleles of different genes assort independently during gamete formation when the genes are unlinked or sufficiently far apart
options.D: Dominant alleles always mask recessive alleles

questions.explanation: Mendel's law of independent assortment states that alleles of different genes assort independently during gamete formation when the genes are unlinked or sufficiently far apart on the same chromosome.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the classic phenotypic ratio in a typical monohybrid cross (Aa x Aa)?
questions.explanation: A typical Aa x Aa cross gives a 3:1 dominant-to-recessive phenotype ratio under complete dominance and simple Mendelian assumptions.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the classic phenotypic ratio in a dihybrid cross (AaBb x AaBb) with independent assortment?
questions.explanation: For AaBb x AaBb with independent assortment and complete dominance, the classic phenotypic ratio is 9:3:3:1.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is genotype?

options.A: The observable characteristics of an organism
options.B: The genetic constitution or allele combination of an organism

questions.explanation: Genotype is the genetic constitution or allele combination of an organism for a gene or set of genes.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is phenotype?

options.A: The genetic constitution of an organism
options.B: The observable characteristics of an organism, resulting from genotype, environment and their interaction

questions.explanation: Phenotype refers to the observable characteristics of an organism, resulting from genotype, environment and their interaction.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is homozygous?

options.A: Having two different alleles of a gene at a locus
options.B: Having two identical alleles of a gene at a locus, such as AA or aa
options.C: Having no alleles for a gene
options.D: Having three alleles for a gene

questions.explanation: Homozygous means having two identical alleles of a gene at a locus, such as AA or aa.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is heterozygous?

options.A: Having two identical alleles of a gene at a locus
options.B: Having two different alleles of a gene at a locus, such as Aa
options.C: Having no alleles for a gene
options.D: Having three alleles for a gene

questions.explanation: Heterozygous means having two different alleles of a gene at a locus, such as Aa.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How is chromosomal sex determined in most humans?

options.A: XX in females and XY in males; the sperm contributes either an X or Y chromosome
options.B: XY in females and XX in males
options.D: Sex is determined by environmental factors only

questions.explanation: Chromosomal sex in most humans is typically XX in females and XY in males; the sperm contributes either an X or Y chromosome, while the egg normally contributes X.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is sex-linked inheritance?

options.A: Inheritance of traits determined by genes on autosomes
options.B: Inheritance of traits determined by genes on sex chromosomes, especially the X chromosome
options.C: Inheritance of traits determined by mitochondrial DNA only
options.D: Inheritance of traits determined by environment

questions.explanation: Sex-linked inheritance is the inheritance of traits determined by genes on sex chromosomes, especially the X chromosome; examples include red-green colour vision deficiency and haemophilia A.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a mutation?

options.A: A change in the DNA sequence or chromosome structure/number
options.B: The normal transmission of genetic information

questions.explanation: A mutation is a change in the DNA sequence or chromosome structure/number; mutations may be neutral, harmful or beneficial and provide raw material for evolution.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is Down syndrome?

options.A: A chromosomal condition most commonly caused by trisomy 21
options.B: An X-linked bleeding disorder

questions.explanation: Down syndrome is a chromosomal condition most commonly caused by trisomy 21, meaning an extra copy of chromosome 21.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is haemophilia?

options.A: An inherited bleeding disorder caused by deficiency or dysfunction of clotting factors
options.B: An inherited disorder of haemoglobin

questions.explanation: Haemophilia is a group of inherited bleeding disorders caused by deficiency or dysfunction of clotting factors; haemophilia A involves factor VIII and haemophilia B factor IX, commonly with X-linked inheritance.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is sickle-cell disease?

options.A: An inherited haemoglobin disorder, usually caused by a variant in the HBB gene that produces haemoglobin S
options.B: A chromosomal condition caused by trisomy 21
options.D: A disorder caused by a lack of vitamin D

questions.explanation: Sickle-cell disease is an inherited haemoglobin disorder, usually caused by a variant in the HBB gene that produces haemoglobin S; red cells can become sickle-shaped under low-oxygen conditions.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is thalassemia?

options.A: A group of inherited disorders with reduced or absent production of alpha- or beta-globin chains
options.B: A chromosomal condition caused by trisomy 21
options.D: A disorder caused by vitamin deficiency

questions.explanation: Thalassemia is a group of inherited disorders with reduced or absent production of alpha- or beta-globin chains, causing anaemia of variable severity.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How are ABO blood groups inherited?

options.A: They are determined mainly by three common alleles where I^A and I^B are codominant and both are dominant over i
options.B: They are determined by a single allele only
options.C: They are determined by environmental factors

questions.explanation: ABO blood groups are determined mainly by three common alleles: I^A and I^B are codominant, and both are dominant over i.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is evolution?

options.A: Change in heritable characteristics of populations over successive generations
options.B: The development of an individual organism
options.D: The transmission of traits from parents to offspring

questions.explanation: Evolution is change in heritable characteristics of populations over successive generations; it explains the diversity and common ancestry of life.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is Darwin's theory of natural selection?

options.A: Individuals with heritable traits that improve survival or reproductive success tend to leave more offspring, so those traits become more common over generations
options.B: All organisms evolve at the same rate

questions.explanation: Darwin's theory of natural selection states that individuals with heritable traits that improve survival or reproductive success in a particular environment tend to leave more offspring, so those traits can become more common over generations.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is an adaptation?

options.A: An inherited feature that improves an organism's survival or reproductive success in a particular environment
options.B: A change acquired during an individual's lifetime
options.C: A type of mutation that is always harmful
options.D: The process of natural selection only

questions.explanation: An adaptation is an inherited feature that improves an organism's survival or reproductive success in a particular environment; adaptation occurs across generations, not because an individual consciously changes.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are fossils?

options.A: Living organisms preserved in ice
options.B: Preserved remains, impressions or traces of ancient organisms, commonly found in sedimentary rocks
options.D: Organisms that have not changed over time

questions.explanation: Fossils are preserved remains, impressions or traces of ancient organisms, commonly found in sedimentary rocks; they provide evidence about past life and evolution.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What was the Miller-Urey experiment?

options.A: An experiment that created life from non-living matter
options.B: A 1953 experiment that simulated early-Earth conditions and produced amino acids and other organic compounds from simple gases and electrical sparks
options.C: An experiment that proved the theory of natural selection
options.D: An experiment that discovered the structure of DNA

questions.explanation: The Miller-Urey experiment was a 1953 experiment by Stanley Miller and Harold Urey that simulated some proposed early-Earth conditions and produced amino acids and other organic compounds from simple gases and electrical sparks; it did not create life.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are the major traditional groups in plant classification?

options.A: Algae, bryophytes, pteridophytes, gymnosperms and angiosperms
options.B: Mosses, ferns, fungi and animals
options.C: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia

questions.explanation: The major traditional groups in plant classification are algae, bryophytes, pteridophytes, gymnosperms and angiosperms; fungi are not plants in modern classification.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are bryophytes?

options.A: Small non-vascular land plants such as mosses and liverworts
options.B: Seedless vascular plants such as ferns
options.C: Seed-producing vascular plants with naked seeds

questions.explanation: Bryophytes are small non-vascular land plants such as mosses and liverworts; they lack true vascular tissues and usually require water for fertilisation.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Why are bryophytes called amphibians of the plant kingdom?

options.A: Because they live only in water
options.B: Because they are mainly terrestrial but require water for the movement of flagellated sperm during sexual reproduction
options.C: Because they have true vascular tissues

questions.explanation: Bryophytes are called amphibians of the plant kingdom because they are mainly terrestrial but require water for the movement of flagellated sperm during sexual reproduction.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are pteridophytes?

options.A: Non-vascular land plants
options.B: Seedless vascular plants such as ferns and horsetails
options.C: Seed-producing vascular plants with naked seeds

questions.explanation: Pteridophytes are seedless vascular plants such as ferns and horsetails; they possess xylem and phloem and reproduce by spores.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are gymnosperms?

options.A: Seed-producing vascular plants whose seeds are not enclosed in fruits
options.B: Flowering plants whose seeds are enclosed within an ovary

questions.explanation: Gymnosperms are seed-producing vascular plants whose seeds are not enclosed in fruits; examples include pine, cycas and fir.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are angiosperms?

options.A: Seed-producing vascular plants with naked seeds
options.B: Flowering plants whose seeds are enclosed within an ovary that usually develops into a fruit

questions.explanation: Angiosperms are flowering plants whose seeds are enclosed within an ovary that usually develops into a fruit.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the difference between monocots and dicots?

options.A: Monocots typically have one cotyledon, parallel leaf venation, fibrous roots and floral parts in threes; eudicots typically have two cotyledons, net venation, taproots and floral parts in fours or fives
options.B: Monocots have two cotyledons; dicots have one
options.C: Monocots have net venation; dicots have parallel venation
options.D: There is no difference between monocots and dicots

questions.explanation: Monocots typically have one cotyledon, parallel leaf venation, fibrous roots and floral parts in threes; eudicots typically have two cotyledons, net venation, taproots and floral parts in fours or fives, with exceptions.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a plant cell wall mainly made of?

options.A: Chitin
options.B: Cellulose, together with hemicelluloses and pectins

questions.explanation: A plant cell wall is mainly made of cellulose, together with hemicelluloses and pectins; secondary walls may also contain lignin.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are meristematic tissues?

options.A: Mature tissues that perform functions such as storage and transport
options.B: Regions of actively dividing plant cells responsible for growth
options.C: Tissues that cover the outer surface of the plant
options.D: Tissues that conduct water and minerals

questions.explanation: Meristematic tissues are regions of actively dividing plant cells responsible for growth; apical meristems increase length, lateral meristems increase girth and intercalary meristems support growth at nodes or leaf bases in some plants.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are the main simple permanent tissues in plants?

options.A: Parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma
options.B: Xylem, phloem and cambium

questions.explanation: The main simple permanent tissues are parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is parenchyma?

options.A: A living, relatively thin-walled tissue involved in storage, photosynthesis and repair
options.B: A supporting tissue with unevenly thickened cell walls
options.C: A supporting tissue with thick, lignified walls
options.D: A tissue that conducts water and minerals

questions.explanation: Parenchyma is a living, relatively thin-walled tissue involved in storage, photosynthesis and repair; chlorenchyma is photosynthetic parenchyma.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is collenchyma?

options.A: A living supporting tissue with unevenly thickened cell walls, providing flexible support in growing plant parts
options.B: A dead supporting tissue with lignified walls

questions.explanation: Collenchyma is a living supporting tissue with unevenly thickened cell walls, providing flexible support in growing plant parts.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is sclerenchyma?

options.A: A living tissue with thin walls
options.B: A supporting tissue with thick, usually lignified walls; mature fibres and sclereids are generally dead

questions.explanation: Sclerenchyma is a supporting tissue with thick, usually lignified walls; mature fibres and sclereids are generally dead.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are the main functions of roots?

options.A: Photosynthesis and gas exchange
options.B: Anchorage, absorption of water and minerals, storage and sometimes vegetative propagation

questions.explanation: The main functions of roots are anchorage, absorption of water and minerals, storage in some plants and sometimes vegetative propagation.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a taproot system?

options.A: A root system with one main primary root and lateral branches
options.B: A cluster of similarly sized roots arising near the stem base
options.C: A root system that grows above ground
options.D: A root system found only in monocots

questions.explanation: A taproot system has one main primary root and lateral branches; it is common in many dicots such as mustard and carrot.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a fibrous root system?

options.A: A root system with one main primary root
options.B: A cluster of similarly sized roots arising near the stem base
options.C: A root system found only in dicots
options.D: A root system that stores water

questions.explanation: A fibrous root system is a cluster of similarly sized roots arising near the stem base; it is common in many monocots such as grasses and rice.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are the main functions of the stem?

options.A: Photosynthesis and gas exchange
options.B: Support, positioning of leaves and flowers, transport through vascular tissues and sometimes storage and vegetative propagation

questions.explanation: The main functions of the stem are support, positioning of leaves and flowers, transport through vascular tissues and, in some plants, storage and vegetative propagation.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are the main functions of leaves?

options.A: Support and transport only
options.B: Photosynthesis, gas exchange and transpiration

questions.explanation: The main functions of leaves are photosynthesis, gas exchange and transpiration; leaves may be modified for storage, protection or climbing.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are stomata?

options.A: Small pores in the epidermis, usually controlled by guard cells, that regulate gas exchange and water vapour loss
options.B: Structures that absorb water from the soil

questions.explanation: Stomata are small pores in the epidermis, usually controlled by guard cells, that regulate gas exchange and water vapour loss.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the male reproductive part of a typical flower?

options.A: The carpel or pistil
options.B: The stamen, consisting of anther and filament

questions.explanation: The male reproductive part of a typical flower is the stamen, consisting of anther and filament; the anther produces pollen grains.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the female reproductive part of a typical flower?

options.A: The stamen
options.B: The carpel or pistil, consisting of stigma, style and ovary

questions.explanation: The female reproductive part of a typical flower is the carpel or pistil, consisting of stigma, style and ovary; ovules are present inside the ovary.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a fruit?

options.A: A mature ovary, usually formed after fertilisation, that protects seeds and can aid seed dispersal
options.B: A mature ovule containing an embryo
options.C: The male reproductive structure of a flower

questions.explanation: A fruit is a mature ovary, usually formed after fertilisation; it protects seeds and can aid seed dispersal. Some fruits include accessory tissues.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a seed?

options.A: A mature fertilised ovule containing an embryo, stored food in many species and a protective seed coat
options.B: A mature ovary containing seeds
options.C: The male reproductive structure of a flower

questions.explanation: A seed is a mature fertilised ovule containing an embryo, stored food in many species and a protective seed coat.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is photosynthesis?

options.A: The process by which plants, algae and some bacteria convert light energy into chemical energy, using carbon dioxide and water to synthesise organic compounds and releasing oxygen
options.B: The process of breaking down glucose to release energy
options.C: The loss of water vapour from leaves
options.D: The transport of sugars through phloem

questions.explanation: Photosynthesis is the process by which plants, algae and some bacteria convert light energy into chemical energy, using carbon dioxide and water to synthesise organic compounds; oxygen is released in oxygenic photosynthesis.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Where does photosynthesis occur in plant cells?

options.A: In mitochondria
options.B: In chloroplasts; light-dependent reactions occur in thylakoid membranes and the Calvin cycle occurs in the stroma

questions.explanation: Photosynthesis occurs in chloroplasts; light-dependent reactions occur in thylakoid membranes and the Calvin cycle occurs in the stroma.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is chlorophyll?

options.A: A green pigment in photosynthetic organisms that absorbs light energy
options.B: A hormone that regulates plant growth

questions.explanation: Chlorophyll is a green pigment in photosynthetic organisms that absorbs light energy; chlorophyll is the primary photosynthetic pigment in plants.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are the main factors affecting photosynthesis?

options.A: Only light intensity
options.B: Light intensity and quality, carbon dioxide concentration, temperature, water availability, chlorophyll content and mineral nutrition

questions.explanation: The main factors affecting photosynthesis are light intensity and quality, carbon dioxide concentration, temperature, water availability, chlorophyll content and mineral nutrition.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Do plants respire only at night?

options.A: Yes, plants respire only at night
options.B: No, plants respire continuously, day and night; photosynthesis occurs only when suitable light is available
options.C: Yes, plants respire only during the day
options.D: Plants do not respire at all

questions.explanation: Plants respire continuously, day and night; photosynthesis occurs only when suitable light is available.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is transpiration?

options.A: Loss of water vapour from aerial parts of plants, mainly through stomata
options.B: The transport of sugars through phloem
options.C: The absorption of water by roots

questions.explanation: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from aerial parts of plants, mainly through stomata, with smaller contributions from the cuticle and lenticels.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the transpiration pull?

options.A: The tension generated by evaporation from leaf surfaces that helps pull water upward through xylem
options.B: The pressure that pushes water down through phloem
options.C: The force that pushes sugars into roots

questions.explanation: The transpiration pull is the tension generated by evaporation from leaf surfaces that helps pull water upward through xylem from roots.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is xylem?

options.A: A vascular tissue that transports sugars and other organic substances
options.B: A vascular tissue that conducts water and dissolved mineral ions mainly from roots to aerial parts and provides mechanical support
options.C: A tissue that covers the outer surface of the plant
